editorials.title: Endurance test: On the Indian economy’s resilience
editorials.passage:
India’s economic growth during the first quarter of this financial year has surprised most people. Against a perception among economists that growth would slow to about 6%-7% on account of the impact of the West Asia crisis, real growth in the April-June 2026 quarter came in at a robust 7.8% . This was not a statistical anomaly, either, as growth was underpinned by strong performances in both manufacturing and services. In fact, the manufacturing sector grew at a three-quarter-high of 9.2%. The sector has likely benefited from the Goods and Services Tax rate cut implemented last September, and further from the Reserve Bank of India’s (RBI) 125-basis point cumulative interest rate cuts through 2025. A part of it is also that companies likely front-loaded their output in the expectation of further uncertainty on inflation, potential future rate hikes, and other possible headwinds. The other piece of good news is that capital creation seems to have picked up. While it is not yet clear what the share is between the government and the private sector, capital creation overall has a welcome multiplier effect on the economy. The services sector, too, has continued to see robust growth, adding strength to the economy. Yet, the economy is not out of the woods, and this robust performance will be more difficult to replicate in the quarters ahead. As Chief Economic Adviser V. Anantha Nageswaran has cautioned, Hormuz uncertainty is likely to keep oil prices above $80 a barrel, too high for a country that imports 85%-90% of its oil requirement.

This is perhaps why Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Tuesday reiterated his appeal to Indians to buy local, avoid non-essential foreign travel and weddings abroad, and stop unnecessary purchases of gold. The pressure of maintaining a reasonable trade deficit has so far rested on India’s services exports. This has served India reasonably well so far, but the global economy is stuttering. This, combined with the growth of Artificial Intelligence services elsewhere, could hurt demand for Indian services exports going ahead. The economy is also yet to face the full brunt of a deficient monsoon and the impact this will have on rural demand. The consumption-related data for July in the Index of Industrial Production already points to sluggish rural demand. While inflation remains well within the RBI’s comfort zone, it has been increasing. The RBI expects it to hit 5.9% in October-December 2026, which would further hit demand. The front-loading of manufacturing will also, by definition, peter out over the next few quarters. The strength of the Indian economy’s resilience was tested in Q1 and it passed admirably. However, the much tougher stamina test remains.

editorials.title: Do not gamble: On the Russia-Ukraine conflict
editorials.passage:
With Russia and Ukraine escalating their long-range attacks on each other’s territory, the risk of the conflict spilling over into other parts of Europe is rising. There have been isolated but significant incidents suggesting that Russia is carrying out ‘gray zone’ attacks, testing the resolve of the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation (NATO) . Three explosive drones were discovered near a German airport . One was shot down over Romania, while another Russian projectile landed in Poland . European officials also say that Russia is recruiting foreign agents for sabotage and conducting cyberattacks for digital espionage. According to U.S. media reports, U.S. intelligence agencies believe that Russian President Vladimir Putin, under pressure at home amid Ukraine’s growing long-range attacks, could carry out a cyberattack or a limited land incursion into NATO territory in the years ahead. CIA chief John Ratcliffe visited Moscow in a bid to warn the Kremlin against escalating the war into NATO member-states. Inside Russia, government officials and nationalist voices have hardened their rhetoric. A Foreign Ministry spokesperson recently said British military facilities “located both inside Ukraine and beyond its borders” may become legitimate targets if Ukraine continues to attack Russia with British weapons. Mikhail Galuzin, Russia’s Deputy Foreign Minister, recently threatened to topple the regime in Kyiv and establish a new governance body — all suggesting that Russia could be preparing to escalate the war.

Russia still has no clear path to victory. Yes, Russia has taken more than 20% of Ukraine’s pre-2014 territory. But its incremental territorial gains have slowed. Until early this year, the Russians were using artillery, glide bombs, drones and infantry to blast through Ukraine’s deeply entrenched positions. But with its long-range attacks, particularly on Russia’s energy sector, supply networks, and military systems, Ukraine’s new aerial front is inflicting economic pain on the Russians. According to some reports, Ukrainian attacks have knocked out roughly 20% of Russia’s refining capacity. Russia is also striking Ukraine — its air defences are weak — with drones and ballistic missiles. But with continuing support from Europe, Kyiv has managed to withstand Russia’s hits. But this stalemate is dangerous. Under pressure at home and stuck on the frontline, Russia could use U.S. preoccupation in the Persian Gulf to escalate the conflict and break the impasse. But that would be a huge mistake, as it could trigger an all-out war between two nuclear-armed sides. Escalation would only compound Russia’s problems. Mr. Putin should instead opt for serious diplomatic engagement with Ukraine and the West, to find a middle ground and end Europe’s longest war since the Second World War.

editorials.title: RSS chief continues to indicate moderate line
editorials.passage: Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh chief Mohan Bhagwat’s recent address at a Universal Oneness Celebration conference in New York was all about the spirit of moderation and inclusivity. Flanked by a rabbi, an imam and a reverend, he said diversity has to be celebrated, respected and accepted. Diversity is the rule of nature; unity is the truth behind nature, he emphasised. At an earlier event in the day, Bhagwat had said, “Any Hindu who believes Muslims should be driven out of India cannot remain a Hindu.” The RSS leadership is not known for delivering punchlines. Yet, Bhagwat’s statement stood out for its candour, much like the point he made at a gathering in Mumbai a few weeks ago, where he said he would “trust Gen Z blindly”. Bhagwat admitted that the Sangh was keen on influencing public policy and politics, but said the work has to begin at the level of the society because that’s where the call for change has to come from.None of this exposition was new for Bhagwat, except for the Gen Z mention; the RSS chief has been articulating a softer line on ideological matters for the last five years. One of his earliest one-liners that made analysts take notice was his advice to people to stop looking for a Shivling under every mosque. At the New York address, an anecdote on the 1996 Charkhi Dadri mid-air aircraft collision may not have landed the way he would have expected, but that did not deflect from the fact that RSS volunteers are usually among the first responders in times of natural calamities..Both Bhagwat and Prime Minister Narendra Modi are trying to take the edge off the perception of ideological rigidity by nuancing their public posture. But getting the entire organisation to think and react likewise is not easy. How else does one explain the Madhya Pradesh government’s decision to deny sanction to prosecute Cabinet minister Kunwar Vijay Shah despite his scurrilous remarks against Army officer Colonel Sofiya Qureshi during Operation Sindoor? By design or otherwise, Bhagwat’s trip abroad comes at a time when youth unease over lack of employment is at its peak. Its political fallout is difficult to predict, as there are many moving parts. editorials.title: Broad-based growth needed beyond healthy headline numbers
editorials.passage: India's real GDP growth accelerated to 7.8 percent in the first quarter of 2026-27 from 6.9 percent a year ago, surpassing consensus estimates. The faster-than-expected growth is particularly encouraging amid external headwinds including the US tariff uncertainty and the West Asia conflict. It shows India not only managed to withstand the quarter’s oil shock, but also surprised with a growth upside. However, crude prices, which tore past $121 a barrel in May and will likely remain elevated throughout this fiscal, could throw a spanner in India’s growth story in subsequent quarters. To recall, India was pushed into the so-called Fragile Five emerging market economies more than a decade ago when crude prices crossed $100. So, the markets were anxious that supply disruptions would again unleash the inflationary beast, which, along with the depreciating currency and rising current account deficit, could force the economy into a doom-loop. Instead, India averted the worst fears. The sectoral growth mix rates a mention. Unlike past crises, where government expenditure single-handedly supported the headline GDP number, most key growth levers hummed along at desirable speeds. While agriculture could surely do better, manufacturing and services growth, at about 10 percent each, saw spirited recovery alongside private investments. The Centre’s capital expenditure grew 23.7 percent, while exports exceeded expectations with a 12 percent growth in real terms..That said, sustaining the 7 percent rate over the next three quarters will be a challenge that will need growth momentum to be kept up in private investment, manufacturing and services. External risks such as volatile energy prices, trade fragmentation and unpredictable global demand weigh heavily on India’s overall prospects. So, though the stronger-than-anticipated Q1 growth prompted calls for raising the 2026-27 forecast, caution is warranted. Even though the gap between the real and the nominal GDP growth suggests moderate price pressures at the aggregate level, sector-specific inflation can strain household budgets hereon.Growth is more likely to soften in the second half as demand boost from the GST rate rationalisation gradually fades. Risks also continue to persist from an uneven monsoon and challenging global environment. So, the rest of the fiscal could risk higher inflation, dampening consumption and weakening private investments amid global macroeconomic concerns. Thus, ensuring broad-based growth has now become as critical as achieving a healthy headline number..Follow The New Indian Express channel on WhatsApp Download the TNIE app to stay with us and follow the latest

editorials.title: Quick Take | Mind that substitute
editorials.passage: Those trying to replace sugar with its increasingly popular substitute xylitol would do well to look at a large study recently presented at the world’s most influential heart health conference. A study of 17,710 people, conducted at Berlin’s Charité Medical School and Hospital and presented at the European Society of Cardiology congress in Munich, showed an increased risk of blood clotting, heart attack and strokes among those with higher levels of this low-calorie sugar substitute. Problem is, it’s increasingly used in common items like chewing gums, toothpaste and ice-creams. India, which has the highest incidence of diabetes in the world, must fund extensive studies to ascertain the presence of the substance in food items and its effect under Indian conditions..Follow The New Indian Express channel on WhatsApp Download the TNIE app to stay with us and follow the latest

editorials.title: The Great Compression
editorials.passage:
Nations rarely announce their turning points. They arrive as gazette notifications, addenda to handbooks, and judgments read out on a Friday afternoon. Consider the four that have landed in quick succession. On 21 August 2026, a Supreme Court bench led by Chief Justice Surya Kant modified its own May 2025 verdict and cut the mandatory pre-entry Bar practice for civil judge (junior division) aspirants from three years to one ~ with a full year of judicial academy training and a further year of clerkship, six months under a district judge and six under a sitting High Court judge, bolted on after selection. 

The new regime begins on 1 April 2027. Until 31 March 2027, fresh law graduates may sit the exam with no practice at all, entering service as trainee judicial officers. The decision was 2:1. One judge dissented. In technical education, the four-year BSc (Honours/Research) born of NEP 2020 has been steadily normalised as equivalent to a four-year engineering degree for postgraduate purposes. AICTE- and government-approved four-year BS/BSc holders now appear by name in the eligibility clauses of ME/MTech admissions at institutions including the IITs, subject to GATE and departmental discretion. 

A physics graduate can now walk into a semiconductor materials MTech without first detouring through an MSc. In research, the UGC’s post-2022 architecture allows a four-year undergraduate degree holder with 75 per cent marks (or 7.5 CGPA) to sit NET and enter a PhD directly ~ in any subject, irrespective of the discipline of the bachelor’s degree. The MPhil is gone. The master’s, for the top decile, is now optional. In medicine, competency-based medical education has moved simulation from a showpiece to a requirement, with skills labs, early clinical exposure and mannequin-and-VR training embedded in the curriculum. 

Alongside it, the National Board of Examinations has pushed AI literacy programmes to tens of thousands of postgraduate trainees, the NMC has been folding AI into the foundation course, and in August 2026 a national consultation in Delhi produced a declaration on AI readiness in healthcare and medical education. The NMC’s own chairperson has said the plain thing out loud: India’s problem is no longer the number of medical seats; it is the quality of the doctor at the end of them. 

Four different regulators. Four different professions. One hinge. Every one of these decisions shortens the runway between a young Indian and the point at which they are permitted to be taken seriously. Read together, these are not four reforms. They are a single wager. The wager is that time served is a poor proxy for competence held ~ and that structured, supervised, instrumented training can deliver in one year what unstructured apprenticeship delivered in three, or failed to. This is not a small philosophical shift. India's professional gatekeeping has always been fundamentally temporal. You were qualified because you had waited. 

The junior in chambers, the resident on the wards, the MSc before the MTech, the master’s before the doctorate ~ these were rites of duration. The new logic is evidentiary: you are qualified because you have demonstrably done the thing, under observation, against a competency map. The judiciary’s own compromise is the cleanest statement of it. The Court did not abolish the experience requirement; it re-engineered it. Two years of ambient courtroom exposure were swapped for one year of academy instruction plus a year of clerkship at two levels of the judicial hierarchy. 

That is a deliberate exchange of quantity for design. The same swap is happening in medicine, where a simulated cardiac arrest at 2 a.m. in a skills lab is being treated as pedagogically superior to the possibility of never having seen one during a rotation. And in research, where a four-year UG with a genuine research component is being treated as a better predictor of doctoral capacity than a two-year taught master’s. A demographic year, recovered. India’s median age is around 29 and rising. Every year shaved off the qualification pipeline is a year added to the productive life of a professional ~ multiplied across lakhs of entrants annually. 

Compressed by two or three years each, across law, engineering, research and medicine, this is not a rounding error. It is one of the largest human-capital timing interventions any country has attempted this decade. The three-year Bar practice rule was argued in court to be pushing women out of the judiciary - the years of unpaid or barely-paid junior practice collide precisely with the years of maximum family pressure to marry and exit. Shortening that window is, in effect, a gender intervention wearing the costume of an eligibility clause. Expect the composition of the subordinate judiciary in 2032 to look measurably different from 2022, and expect that to change what gets litigated and how. 

The old system taxed those who could afford to wait. Three unpaid years at the Bar, an extra MSc, an extra master’s ~ each was a wealth filter dressed as a merit filter. Compression is quietly redistributive. The single most under-read line in all four reforms is the UGC’s: a PhD in any subject, regardless of the undergraduate discipline. That sentence licenses an entire generation of legitimate hybrids ~ the economics graduate doing a doctorate in climate modelling, the biology graduate in computational linguistics. 

India's research output has long been strong in volume and thin in genuinely interdisciplinary work. This is the clause that changes that, if the universities let it. A judicial officer appointed at 25 rather than 29 will spend four more years on the bench, and will reach senior positions younger. Multiply that across the civil-adjacent professions and you get a governing class that arrives earlier, stays longer, and was formed by post-2020 institutions rather than pre-liberalisation ones. Whether that produces boldness or brittleness is the central open question of the 2040s. Balance requires naming the failure modes precisely, not gesturing at them. 

Judgement is not a competency. You can certify a doctor’s ability to intubate. You cannot easily certify a judge’s ability to disbelieve a plausible witness. The dissent in the judicial services case rests on a real intuition: courtroom exposure teaches the smell of a case ~ which affidavit is manufactured, which adjournment is tactical, which litigant is desperate. This is tacit knowledge, and tacit knowledge is exactly what structured training is worst at transmitting. A trainee judicial officer who has read about mala fide litigation is not the same instrument as one who has been on the receiving end of it. The reform is only as good as the academy. 

This is the load-bearing risk across all four decisions. The judicial compromise assumes State Judicial Academies of uniform quality ~ they are not uniform. The medical reform assumes functioning simulation labs ~ a well-funded metro institution and a two-year-old private college in a district town are running the same regulation and not the same education. The MTech pathway assumes four-year BSc programmes with real research content ~ many will be three-year programmes with a year of padding. Compression without capacity is not acceleration always; it could be dilution with a shorter timeline. 

The gap between the best and worst institutions, already India’s defining educational fact, will now be measured in readiness at entry rather than years at entry ~ and it will widen before it narrows. Simulated patients do not have unlisted comorbidities, do not lie about their symptoms, do not arrive with three anxious relatives, and do not die. AI decision support is trained on data distributions that under-represent exactly the Indian district-hospital presentations where it will be deployed. A cohort trained to trust the machine, in settings where the machine is out of distribution, is a specific and foreseeable patient-safety problem. 

The right response is not to reverse the reform but to build deliberate disconfirmation into it ~ training that teaches when to override. Credential compression meets credential inflation. If a PhD is reachable four years out of school, the market response is predictable: the PhD becomes the new master’s, and differentiation migrates upward. India could arrive at 2035 with far more doctorates and no more researchers. By 2030, the median age of first appointment in the subordinate judiciary will have dropped by roughly three years, and the share of women in entry-level judicial service will have risen sharply. 

Expect a parallel rise in appellate reversal rates for the 2027-2030 cohorts, and expect that statistic to be weaponised by both sides of the debate before anyone has controlled for case mix. By 2032, the “MTech from a BSc” cohort will be visibly overrepresented in India's semiconductor, materials, quantum and bio-manufacturing programmes ~ precisely the sectors where physics and chemistry training beats conventional engineering training. This will be the most quietly successful of the four reforms. By 2035, India will have a first cohort of researchers who never held a master’s degree ~ and the country will have its first genuine argument about whether the master’s degree was ever load-bearing or merely customary. 

Expect the top institutions to quietly reintroduce a screening layer under a different name. By 2040, the clinician trained under CBME-plus-AI will be a structurally different professional: weaker at unaided differential diagnosis, dramatically stronger at pattern recognition at volume, and dependent on infrastructure. India’s health system will have to decide whether that is a workforce it can deploy in Tier-3 districts or only in Tier-1 cities. By 2047, the composite: a professional class that is younger, less deferential, more interdisciplinary, more instrumented, more mobile - and less internally uniform than any India has produced. 

The old schools do break here. The lineage model of Indian professional life - the chambers, the gurushishya lab, the unit under a professor ~ loses its monopoly on entry. What replaces it is faster and flatter, but also thinner in mentorship, and mentorship is where ethics were historically transmitted. That is the real trade, stated plainly. India has chosen speed and access over apprenticeship and induction. The gains are immediate, measurable and largely real. The costs are delayed, diffuse, and will show up as judgement failures rather than knowledge failures ~ a wrong bail order, a missed atypical presentation, a doctoral thesis that is technically flawless and intellectually inert. 

None of this is fated. The variable is not the reform; it is the scaffolding. Three things decide the outcome. First, whether the training institutions ~ judicial academies, skills labs, four-year UG research components ~ are built to a national floor or left to state and market variation. Second, whether India builds structured mentorship back in deliberately, having removed it accidentally: clerkships that are real, residencies that supervise, doctoral committees that read. 

Third, whether anyone measures. The 2027 judicial cohort, the first BSc-to-MTech batch, the first direct-entry PhDs ~ these are natural experiments with clean control groups. A country that tracks them will course-correct by 2032. A country that does not will discover the answer in 2045, when the cohort is running the institutions. The gate has opened. Whether what walks through is fresh talent or merely young talent depends entirely on what India builds on the other side of it. 

(The writer is a thinker and a technocrat)

editorials.title: But where is India’s economic growth?
editorials.passage:
Even as the freightlines open and the cranes swing over skylines that did not have them, conversations in some circles, typically elite ones, now carry a refrain that has stopped being a question. Whenever the discussion on the Indian economy comes up, someone says: “But where is the growth?” A good quarter might be conceded. One or two sectors might be allowed to have done well. 

But it is quickly followed by the chorus, “Yes, yes. But where is the growth?” The conversation has become a kind of nursery rhyme, and a particularly strange one, because holding on to it now requires an extraordinary act of not looking. There was an economy whose nominal output rose from about Rs 124 lakh crore to around Rs 346 lakh crore in a decade, with exports reaching roughly $860 billion. India has been the fastest-growing major economy for much of this period. 

“Yes, but is that real growth?” There was a banking system whose bad loans, once the books were finally opened honestly, rose above eleven per cent. Banks were called zombies. Gross NPAs are now below two per cent, banks are profitable and credit is expanding. The companies that spent those years repairing themselves are compounding too: the June quarter delivered 18 per cent Nifty profit growth, the best in ten quarters, with nineteen sectors beating estimates and mid-cap and small-cap earnings growing faster still. “But that’s just the stock market.” There was a railway that had electrified barely a fifth of its network in seven decades and has now electrified 99.6 per cent of its broad-gauge network. Consequential train accidents fell from 135 a year to 16. 

Metro rail went from 248 kilometres in five cities to over a thousand across twenty-six. A country with no dedicated freight corridor has now commissioned 2,843 kilometres of one. There were 74 airports; there are now 165. There were 91,287 kilometres of national highways; there are now 1,46,572. “But can a bullock cart use an expressway?” There was a power sector with 2.8 gigawatts of solar. India now has more than 164. Non-fossil sources have crossed half of installed electricity capacity, years ahead of the target India had set itself. Rural electricity supply has risen from 12.5 hours a day to more than 22. A generation is growing up that has never done homework by candlelight. 

“But what will people do with electricity?” Seventeen per cent of rural homes had a tap; the figure is now above eighty. Sanitation went from 39 per cent to near-universal coverage on the back of 12 crore toilets. Medical colleges have gone from 387 to 846, and MBBS seats from 51,348 to nearly 1,40,000. Life expectancy is 72 years, the highest ever recorded here. And by the World Bank's own count, extreme poverty fell from 27.1 per cent to 5.3 per cent between 2011-12 and 2022-23. That is about 269 million people. “But those are schemes, not growth.” There was a payments system that barely existed a decade ago and now handles roughly half of all real-time digital transactions on earth. And 99.2 per cent of the phones sold in India are now made in India, against 26 per cent in 2014-15. 

Electronics went from a marginal export category to one of the country’s largest. Defence exports went from �686 crore to more than �38,000 crore. There was barely an Indian semiconductor story worth telling; now twelve manufacturing projects have been approved, and commercial production has begun at three. “But where is the growth?” Here is what makes the refrain particularly odd right now. Much of the world has, for now, been reduced to a remarkably narrow economic story: AI, AI chips, AI data centres, AI capital expenditure. The same cluster of companies, the same investment cycle, the same trade, over and over. India’s story looks nothing like that. 

There is technology growth, but alongside it there is manufacturing, infrastructure, financial services, renewables, defence, electronics, aviation, rail, construction, pharmaceuticals, automobiles, digital commerce and semiconductors. The point is that there are so many of them. Much of the world is running on one engine. India has several. Growth looks like a semiconductor plant rising where there was an empty field, and another airport appearing on a map that used to be blank. It looks like a bank lending again because its balance sheet is no longer poisoned. 

It also looks like the welder on that freight corridor, and the girl holding the first MBBS seat her village has ever sent anyone to. Like the grandmother who no longer walks two kilometres before dawn for water. Like the small town that got an airport and discovered it was not small. That is growth. What else would it be? Nobody is claiming the work is finished. But the direction is no longer in doubt. Give India one more decade like the last one, and today's forecasts will look timid. One can argue about whether a particular quarter disappointed, whether a project was delayed, whether one sector is overhyped and another underperforming. 

But if GDP, investment, profits, credit , infrastructure, manufacturing, exports and the emergence of entire new industries do not count as evidence of growth, then “Where is the growth?” is a question constructed so that no answer can satisfy it. That is why the refrain survives every answer, and why it deserves none. So, the next time it arrives, look at the tracks, the roads, the factories, and the companies that did not exist ten years ago. Where is the growth? Everywhere you are refusing to look. 

(The writer is an economist and Associate Professor of Finance at SPJIMR. He holds a PhD from IIM Calcutta, an MBA from IIM Calcutta, and a B.Tech (Hons) from IIT Kharagpur. Views are personal.)

editorials.title: Change of guard, change of colour
editorials.passage:
As one of the distinctly visible and integral components of public life, it is extremely difficult to ignore the various shades of colour that glare at us in myriad forms via government buildings, flyovers, road-crossings, viaducts, street railings, hospices, public transport vehicles, parks, gardens, and a host of other civic structures, teeming the urban spaces that we inhabit. As public spaces are accessible to all, the colours chosen for their representation should ideally conform to the needs and requirements of the general public rather than cater to the predilections of the ruling party or the government. 

In August 2026, the iconic Academy of Fine Arts in Kolkata was at the centre of controversy, as its ticket counter served as a venue for a colourful tug of war between saffron and white, triggering accusations of cultural and political arrogation by rival political parties. Such a controversy, coupled with the onslaught of blue and white of the erstwhile ruling government, automatically generates some basic pertinent queries: should colours of various public infrastructure on perpetual display be overtly used for political messaging or should the hues be determined on the basis of relevant scientific, environmental, pragmatic and other aesthetic factors? 

The question is crucial as the value or choice of colour is not merely an ornamental one. On the contrary, the choice embodies a wide range of important issues including luminosity, perceptibility, heat absorption, and a host of other allied factors aligned with the urban set-up of a city. Instead of being implemented arbitrarily, colour choices in public spaces should be entrusted with a properly equipped team consisting of specialists in the field like trained urban planners, builders, colour experts, engineers, environmentalists, urban traffic and safety professionals among others. 

While it is the democratic prerogative of the ruling government to undertake and implement decisions about public infrastructure, particular choices, including colour, must be backed with qualified knowledge rather than a political impulse based on irrational whims, fancies or brusque political agenda. At the heart of implementation of the colour policy should lie the basic understanding of the fact, that though ruling parties change, public infrastructure continues to journey from one regime to another. The whimsicality of the political colour syndrome has plagued different parts of the country and the world at different stages of history. 

In India, besides West Bengal, states like Andhra Pradesh, Uttar Pradesh and Rajasthan had its share of politicised colour obsessions in the recent past. The legendary Communist obsession with red is well known internationally, pervading countries like China, the former Soviet Union and other states. In the context of the present day, legitimate protest as regards colour policy should not be directed towards the choice of a particular colour but should be against the alteration of public structures into emblems of prejudiced visual statement. Each colour has its specific place and precise use in our lives. 

It is also crucial to remember that no individual colour should be stigmatised as representative of a particular political ideology, as colours carry their uniform charm and appeal across generations. Scientific studies should ideally form the basis of selection of a particular shade, especially keeping in mind significant factors like visibility, resilience, relevance to a specific p urp ose, temp erature absorption and a host of other allied significant factors deemed fit for the cause. It is also important to remember that paint carries the baggage of ecological footprint. 

So, in an era of climate change ecologically superior coatings, wherever relevant and desirable, should be effectively utilised. In choice of colours, distinction must also be made of heritage and culturally significant structures from partisan ownerships. A particular hue that carried sacred, cultural or historic associations, does not inevitably become inappropriate for use in the public domain. On similar lines of vindication, a political party cannot claim an exclusive right on a particular colour. The central question to be focused on here is the suitability of the particular shade serving the public function of the chosen space. 

If a colour change implies no verified functional, environmental or architectural validity then wastage of government expenses and other resources is extremely difficult to justify. A colour choice should also be distinctly independent of individual preferences of the stake holders, bureaucrats and political party members and any other individual aligned with the machinery. It is imperative to remember that there should be no generally prearranged political shade fixed for any public infrastructure. Only on the basis of a rational, scientific and democratic policy formulated by the government should the colour policy be implemented for any state. 

The colours should enhance the purpose and function of the relevant enterprise. A speed braker for instance is designed for safety while a government structure should enhance the official and ecological status of the state. The primary safety concern of the speed braker or the designated street railings should not be compromised at any cost by unscientific use of colour. The colours of heritage buildings should mirror their ethos and sanctity. In short, public colour policy should be evidence-based, milieu-sensitive, politically neutral and unbiased. Political monopolization of colours can trigger greater complications in the long run. 

When a party colour becomes synonymous with a government property, the substituting government may be involuntarily coerced to repaint it in order to remove the visual identity of its predecessor. So, it is high time that an autonomous, independent, scientific colour policy is put in place, especially keeping in mind the challenging environmental requirements of the present world. 

(The writer is the Head, Department of English, St Xavier’s College (Autonomous), Kolkata)

editorials.title: Beyond Victory
editorials.passage:
A hundred days is too short to judge a government, but long enough to understand its instincts. By that measure, the BJP’s first months in power in West Bengal have revealed both the possibilities and the limits of regime change. The change in political atmosphere has been unmistakable. A party that spent decades on Bengal's margins now governs with an authority that would once have been unimaginable. Institutions long identified with the Left-liberal political culture, most conspicuously Jadavpur University, have become arenas for an assertion of a new ideological confidence. 

Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari’s language of nationalism and his challenge to what he calls a culture of intimidation underline a larger ambition: not merely to replace the Trinamool Congress in office, but to alter Bengal’s political vocabulary. That transformation is easier to announce than to accomplish. Bengal’s political culture was not created by Mamata Banerjee alone, nor will it disappear with her electoral defeat. Attempts to impose a new ideological consensus risk producing unnecessary confrontation where a democratic government should instead demonstrate confidence enough to accommodate dissent. Yet it would be equally simplistic to dismiss the new administration as merely symbolic. 

The transfer of long-pending land for border infrastructure and efforts to reconnect Bengal with central schemes show how a change of government can unblock decisions stalled by political conflict. Industrial incentives and investment proposals point to a recognition that Bengal’s real crisis is economic. Here lies the real test. For years, Bengal has suffered from the consequences of industrial decline, inadequate private investment and the outward migration of many of its most employable young people. These problems cannot be solved by renaming schemes, changing official symbols or winning ideological battles on university campuses. 

Nor can investment announcements be confused with factories, or memoranda with jobs. The BJP inherited these structural difficulties. It cannot reasonably be expected to reverse them in 100 days. But its enormous electoral mandate has also removed the excuse of political weakness. The question now is whether it can convert the authority it has acquired into the administrative consistency investors require. There is a particular danger in confusing political conquest with successful governance. The destruction of an old political order is not the same as building a new economic one. Bengal has seen enough governments that were powerful in politics but disappointing in development. 

The early months suggest a government energetic, ambitious and determined to leave its mark. Its strongest achievements so far have come where the executive's will can quickly remove obstacles. Its greatest promises, however, remain works in progress. That is not yet a failure. But neither is it a success. The real measure of this government will not be how thoroughly it changes the symbols of power, but whether young Bengalis can eventually find reason to build their futures at home. Political victories are won at the ballot box. Economic renewal is earned much more slowly

editorials.title: Owning tradition
editorials.passage:
A jewellery advertisement featuring actor Kriti Sanon has been withdrawn after criticism over her clothes while celebrating Rakshabandhan. What might ordinarily have been a forgettable piece of festive advertising instead became another argument about an unusually persistent Indian question: who gets to decide what a woman should wear? The criticism was not simply that Sanon’s outfit was unsuitable for an advertisement. It was presented as evidence of insufficient respect for a Hindu festival. 

Actor and BJP MP Kangana Ranaut ~ not celebrated for temperance ~ questioned why anyone would celebrate Rakshabandhan in an outfit she considered too revealing. Others objected to Sanon tying a Rakhi to her pet. Supporters, including Congress leader Rahul Gandhi, defended her right to choose what she wore and accused her critics of moral policing. There is nothing inherently unreasonable about finding an outfit inappropriate for a particular occasion. Festivals have cultural codes, families have expectations and individuals are entitled to dislike a fashion choice. The problem begins when personal or community preference is converted into a rule about a woman’s character, cultural loyalty or right to participate in tradition. 

 response went to the heart of that distinction. Her argument was that respect for culture cannot be measured by a neckline. That is an uncomfortable proposition for a society accustomed to judging women through appearance. Indian women have repeatedly encountered this policing in different forms. A student wearing shorts has been told to cover her legs. Women in ripped jeans have been publicly criticised. Beauty contestants wearing Western clothes have faced intimidation. Film actors have routinely been judged for what they wear, while their male counterparts rarely face an equivalent demand to demonstrate cultural respect through their clothing. 

Traditions survive not because every participant dresses identically, but because people continue to find meaning in them. Rakshabandhan is ultimately about a relationship and the emotions attached to it. Whether an individual believes those emotions should extend to a pet is open to debate. But that debate does not require a verdict on a woman’s modesty. The more troubling development is the ease with which outrage can pressure institutions into retreat. The withdrawal of the advertisement may have been a commercial calculation, but some would argue that the publicity ~ adverse though it was ~ only increased brand recognition. But there is a larger principle at stake. 

A woman does not surrender her autonomy because she enters a temple, celebrates a festival or appears in an advertisement invoking tradition. Respect for culture should be a matter of conviction, not a dress code imposed by strangers. India can preserve its traditions without policing women’s bodies. Indeed, a confident culture should be secure enough to accommodate differences. And a nation beset with several serious problems ought not to get sidetracked by such sartorial distractions.

editorials.title: Nature’s fury
editorials.passage:
The gigantic wave of black-brown ice water, rock, sand and debris that swallowed villages, townships, border posts, large trucks, SUVs and people as if they were mere insects along the Nepal-Tibet border could be described as the fist of god, pulverising everything that stood in its path. Indeed, all of us have seen and been shaken by the images of tiny human figures running desperately from the tsunami that was to obliterate them in seconds as it overwhelmed a seven-storey, fancy immigration building.

Like others worldwide, I’ve been watching videos and accounts of the disaster from many sources. What is striking is the vastness of the attack by nature. No human security shield is capable of withstanding an assault of this nature.

An Italian traveller, who scrambled to higher ground with his tour group, described the roar of the river of mud and devastation as the “sound of death”. There are stories also of heroic rescues, of miraculous escapes of people buried in mud and stuck in the turbine tunnels of hydropower dams, and of dogs faithfully waiting in devastated homes for their owners. Thousands across the world wait forlornly for word from their loved ones even as cremation pyres burn in different parts of Nepal. The mourners span the world, from as distant as the United States of America and New Zealand to as close as China and India.

While this catastrophe dwarfs the flood disaster of July in Nagaland and Assam which carried away over 100 persons, there are crucial underlying problems which assert some similarities. These are connected to changing weather patterns, global warming and climate change.

What was extraordinary about the Upper Assam floods is that these happened in the districts of Sivasagar and Charaideo, which do not have a history of flooding. According to World Weather Attribution, which has partnerships with the Imperial College London, the Royal Netherlands Meteorological Institute and the Red Cross Red Crescent Climate Change Centre, multiple spells of heavy to extremely heavy rainfall over two months (between June and August) in Upper Assam as well as “the surrounding hill catchments of Nagaland and Arunachal Pradesh… triggered repeated waves of flash flooding and widespread inundation”. Scientists, officials, witnesses and researchers with whom I have spoken in Nagaland and Assam agree that intense rainfall set off the major devastation in the third week of July. The topsoil and the lower layers of earth got “completely saturated and the hillsides, under the pressure of continuous rain and water accumulation, collapsed”, said one geologist.

In addition, villagers, activists and media in both states have blamed a well-organised mining network involving politicians, contractors, businessmen and local persons of extensive excavation of soil and rock without permission or oversight. This had a role in the Assam disaster, they say, especially as mining has taken place with impunity, damaging the environment. Scientists and academics who have studied the Brahmaputra river basin say that this, and the earlier decades of coal mining that scarred the hills in Nagaland upland of Sivasagar, would have been a contributory factor to the scale of the flood. But they held that the key was excessive downpour (nearly 500% over normal precipitation) — a reflection of climate change. The extraction of sand, silt, rock and stones from streams and riverbeds — a corrupt, illegal practice — is especially harmful since this means that there are no ‘speed barriers’ to the river at a time of spate: the water moves much more swiftly without the slowing effect of sand and stones.

The World Weather Attribution report also cited other factors, including changing land-use patterns: “Evidence from a review of 35 studies suggests that unplanned urbanization, deforestation, poor drainage, inadequate structural flood management measures, and other anthropogenic changes… have degraded wetlands, accelerated riverbank erosion, and disrupted natural drainage, increasing the severity and downstream impacts of flooding.” Private relief groups, NGOs as well as government agencies swept into action to rescue the vulnerable, although the degree of livelihood, crop and household loss was on a scale that, survivors say, would take years to recover.

Both the disaster in Nepal and the flood in Nagaland-Assam underline a few factors which have not been addressed even though nature has sent repeated warnings through the fragile ecosystems of the high Himalayas as well as the lower hills and rivers. One lesson is that climate change is here, and here to stay. That means that we should be prepared for more incidents of intense weather, rain, storms and high floods, whether caused by a crumbling glacier thousands of metres high in the mountains, glacial lakes at risk of exploding, intense rain that triggers landslides or speeding high water in vulnerable areas.

A second is that there is a need to pause all major infrastructure projects in the entire Himalayan-Tibet belt, including ambitious four-lane and six-lane highways that do little but bolster the egos and purses of politicians and their favoured contractors. They trigger landslides, killing dozens of people across the Himalayan region and the eastern hills. A former Sikkim minister has demanded the scrapping of all hydroelectric projects in his state, fearing a Nepal-like calamity.

Third, this is both a wake-up call and a good time for regional collaboration, a phrase and a practice that have fallen into disuse in these past years. Specialists from all countries — China, India, Nepal, Bhutan, Pakistan and Bangladesh — must sit together to assess the risks and map protection plans. After all, if a disaster of this magnitude doesn’t help us cooperate, what will? An attack by nature doesn’t respect borders, doesn’t distinguish between the innocent and the villainous, and can do more damage than most conventional bombs.

Fourth, where are the early warning systems to tell communities downstream of the need to evacuate to safe, higher ground? Do they even exist? The Himalayan region is also a high-risk earthquake zone with large, medium and small cities and populations located on or near fault lines. A combination of an earthquake and a flood would be too frightening to even conceive. The governments of the region (including the states of the Northeast) need to address this question: are they ready for such calamities? If so, where are the plans? They need to be made public, for this is in the public interest.

Governments need to respond with transparency and urgency. These recent incidents have left millions wondering if authorities and official systems are capable of protecting them. This is where public-spirited leaders (they do exist!), professional media outlets (not the godi ones), social media, researchers and scientists need to work together. People have the right to life, not just to survival.

Sanjoy Hazarika is a writer who specialises on the Northeast and travels extensively in the region

editorials.title: Letters to the editor: The West is obsessing over new welless trend ‘Laxmi-maxxing’
editorials.passage:
Sir — The West has been won by a new trend inspired by India’s spiritual traditions. ‘Laxmi-maxxing’ — an attempt to maximise beauty and aura, drawing inspiration from the imagery and the symbolism associated with the eponymous Hindu goddess — has been popularised by a TikToker who is also an ayurvedic practitioner. Yet the trend seems less like an engagement with spirituality than a repackaging of it into wellness. Lakshmi is not simply a symbol of abundance but is associated with a deep-rooted religious tradition. When that association is stripped of its cultural aspect and turned into a set of beauty tips and self-care goals, something is lost. A line must be drawn between cultural appreciation and cultural appropriation.

Sir — The New York address of the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh chief, Mohan Bhagwat, reminds me of the Hindi proverb, ‘ Haathi ke daant khaane ke kuch aur, dikhane ke kuch aur hote hain ’ — roughly translated as ‘One set of the elephant’s teeth is for display, another for chewing’ (“Bhagwat ‘diversity’ counter in US”, Aug 31). There seems to be a clear difference between words and actions.

Avinash Godboley, Dewas, Madhya Pradesh

Sir — After declaring that everyone born in India is a Hindu, the RSS chief appears to have made a remarkable somersault on foreign soil. While addressing a gathering at Madison Square Garden recently, Mohan Bhagwat said that anyone who believes that no Muslim should live in India is not a Hindu. His volte-face may stem from concerns that the RSS, which has often faced allegations of hostility towards minorities, could come under greater criticism abroad. There has also been resentment over Bhagwat’s visit to the United States of America. The recent student protests may have caused concern within the RSS.

Tharcius S. Fernando, Chennai

Sir — Mohan Bhagwat’s assertions at Madison Square Garden are hypocritical. You cannot build an image through words when the facts scream a different story. If Muslims indeed belong to India, as Bhagwat claims, why are they being treated as second-class citizens in their homeland?

Muslims are being systematically marginalised in economic, social, cultural and educational spheres. Cow vigilantes continue to attack Muslims. Mosques and madrasas are targeted. Groups associated with the sangh parivar face allegations of violence against minorities. India does not need sermons on diversity delivered in New York.

Sir — It is distressing to note that some protesters disrespected India’s national flag while opposing Mohan Bhagwat’s speech in New York. Criticism is a legitimate right in a democracy. But insulting the national flag is an insult to the country and its citizens. Those who disrespected the Tricolour should be taken to task.

N.R. Ramachandran, Chennai

Sir — The RSS chief’s celebration of pluralism in the US is a masterclass in doublespeak. It is ironic that an organisation driving an exclusionary, majoritarian agenda at home comfortably adopts the language of universal oneness abroad. This rhetoric cannot mask structural contradictions. While Bhagwat has claimed that diversity is in India’s DNA, his organisation’s actions tell a completely different story. If the RSS leadership genuinely believes in diversity, it should drill this lesson into its cadre rather than package it for a wealthy foreign audience.

Sir — The sangh parivar is more interested in dividing people. The latest example is the controversy over “ Vande Mataram ”. If the RSS has genuinely arrived at a better understanding of the idea of India, the shift must be welcomed. Bhagwat had once advised his cadre not to go in search of a shivling under every Muslim place of worship, but that has not stopped the trend. It remains to be seen how his latest stance is received by RSS cadre.

Sir — The football legend, Lionel Messi, announcing his retirement from international football marks the saddest day for millions of sports lovers across the globe (“Final whistle blown. The artist retires”, Sept 1). For nearly two decades, Messi carried the dreams of a nation and the hopes of the world on his shoulders with breathtaking grace.

Messi made us believe in the impossible every time the ball met his feet. From the heartbreak of his early years to the tears of redemption when he finally lifted the World Cup in 2022, we lived his journey with him. It is hard to imagine a world where we won’t see him glide past defenders in that iconic blue and white jersey again.

Ranganathan Sivakumar, Chennai

Sir — Lionel Messi’s retirement brings an end to his celebrated career with the Argentina national team. Messi became the first footballer in history to record 1,300 goal contributions. Following the announcement, fans flooded social media platforms with emotional farewell messages, thanking him for two decades of historic moments and for setting new benchmarks in the sport.

Sir — The all-time football great, Lionel Messi, has retired from international football at the age of 39. The move was expected given his age. Messi proved his dominance by winning the 2022 World Cup, an Olympic gold medal and the Copa América for Argentina. He created a golden era for world football with his effortless technique, showing the world that a well-played football match can resemble a ballet performance.

editorials.title: Legacy soiled
editorials.passage:
West Bengal has long taken pride in its intellectual tradition. For generations, the state has produced distinguished scholars, scientists, and public intellectuals whose contributions have established Bengal as one of India’s most revered centres of learning. However, today, this proud legacy stands at a crossroads as more than half of the state’s youth struggles to realise their full potential. According to the ILO’s India Employment Report 2024 , nearly 20.21% of the state’s educated youth are unemployed while nearly 34.40% are not in employment, education, or training. This despite the state being home to nearly 1,588 colleges — the tenth-highest number in the country (AISHE 2023-24).

The situation becomes even more concerning given Bengal’s significant demographic advantage. West Bengal is home to approximately 6.9% of the country’s youth population — the fourth highest after Uttar Pradesh (18.6%), Bihar (9.5%), and Maharashtra (8.7%), according to the India Employment Report 2024 . With nearly 26.2% of its population in the 15-29 age group, the state possesses a demographic advantage that many ageing economies, such as those of the United States of America, China, and Japan, can only envy. However, the benefits of this demographic dividend cannot be realised automatically: it must be supported by a higher education system that is capable of producing industry-ready talent. This is where Bengal’s challenge lies.

An analysis of the India Skills Report (2014-2025) reveals a steady weakening of West Bengal’s employability performance relative to other Indian states. While states such as Uttar Pradesh, Delhi, Andhra Pradesh, and Maharashtra have emerged as consistent leaders in employability, West Bengal has remained well below the high-performing group. More concerningly, the state’s employability performance has been marked by considerable inconsistency. For instance, after achieving an impressive second position nationally in 2019, it disappeared entirely from the top 10 employability rankings in 2023, 2024, and 2025.

From an employer’s perspective, this instability raises serious concerns about Bengal’s ability to serve as a reliable source of job-ready talent. This explains why the state has not featured among employers’ preferred hiring destinations since 2022, according to the India Skills Report (2022-2025). In contrast, states such as Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Maharashtra, and Delhi have consistently remained among the top five states preferred by recruiters. Even before 2022, Bengal rarely featured among the top five hiring preferences of employers, with these positions largely occupied by the same states.

The consequences are equally visible among students. A secondary analysis of India Skills Report (2014-2025) reveals that West Bengal has not been among the preferred states for work among youth since 2020. Even earlier, the state appeared among the top 10 preferred work destinations only twice — in 2017 and 2019 — and occupied the tenth position on both occasions. Declining student confidence in employment prospects has contributed to their reduced participation in the state’s higher education system. According to AISHE 2023-24, West Bengal’s gross enrolment ratio in higher education stood at 24.6% compared to the national average of 30%.

This crisis deserves urgent attention because West Bengal’s demographic opportunity is not unlimited. The state’s youth population is projected to decline to 19.6% by 2036 (ILO, 2024), leaving a narrow window to convert its human capital into economic strength. The priority, therefore, must be to ensure that higher education produces not just graduates but employable talent capable of driving Bengal’s future growth.

Aastha Agarwal is Assistant Professor of Political Science, Kolkata Police Law Institute

editorials.title: Sane voice: Editorial on India’s diplomatic role amid wars in Iran and Ukraine
editorials.passage:
The Shanghai Cooperation Organisation’s summit on Monday and Tuesday offered India a valuable platform for Prime Minister Narendra Modi to underscore the country’s positions on key diplomatic priorities — such as the wars raging in Iran and Ukraine and the fight against terrorism. When large groupings like the SCO — comprising China, Russia, India, Pakistan, Iran, Belarus, Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Tajikistan and the host, Kyrgyz Republic — meet, the main conclave can often take on a largely ceremonial role. But meetings held on the sidelines, and comments made by leaders, give countries opportunities to engage in valuable networking on significant issues. In Bishkek, Mr Modi appears to have seized those moments. In his meeting with the Iranian president, Masoud Pezeshkian, the Indian leader emphasised that New Delhi was keen to not only continue trading with Tehran but also actually amplify and widen bilateral trade. Those comments were a significant message to the United States of America whose president and administration have threatened nations with harsh economic penalties for trading with Iran. Again, while meeting the Russian president, Vladimir Putin, Mr Modi spoke of the need to end the war on Ukraine, emphasising how India remained committed to supporting diplomatic efforts that can help seal a peace agreement between Moscow and Kyiv. At a moment when Russia appears to be spurning Ukrainian offers for diplomacy, and with the war escalating, Mr Modi’s words will be welcomed in most parts of the world.

Mr Modi also took on Pakistan’s support for cross-border terrorism, underlining the need for the world to unite against this menace — especially when used by a country as a matter of State policy. Admittedly, these comments by themselves would not move the needle on wars that show no signs of ending; neither would they stop Pakistan from using State-sponsored terrorism against India. But at a time when the world is in greater flux than at any point since the end of the Cold War, with multiple conflicts raging simultaneously, countries around the globe are seeking voices of sanity and maturity. India has the historical, economic and diplomatic heft to serve as one such anchor in choppy waters. New Delhi must act on Mr Modi’s words in Bishkek — demonstrating that while it prefers peace, India can also help the world deal with the consequences of war.

editorials.title: Well done: Editorial on India's 7.8% GDP growth and challenges ahead
editorials.passage:
Global conflicts and their resultant economic turmoil had led to speculation that India’s GDP growth in the first quarter of the current financial year would be a whimper. Instead, India’s GDP, data from the National Statistics Office have shown, has grown with a bang. A rate of 7.8% amidst the economic headwinds is as surprising as it is commendable. It has even surpassed the projection of the Reserve Bank of India. A closer scrutiny would reveal that industry, manufacturing, services and, hearteningly, private consumption have served as the engines of this progress. There are glimpses of promise from within these sectors as well. For instance, within industry, manufacturing, at 9.2%, and construction, at 7.7%, maintained an impressive pace of growth. The consequent harvest has been rich. For manufacturing firms, the margin of operating profits increased from 9.4% to 21.3%; the corresponding gains for IT as well as non-IT services have been robust too. Private consumption, at 7.1%, was egged on by high returns from goods and services tax, income tax concessions, State interventions to minimise the pitfalls of the West Asia crisis and so on. This augurs well for the festive season that is round the corner.

These encouraging numbers underscore the Indian economy’s resilience. The question is whether the momentum will hold. There is, unfortunately, no assurance given the stiff challenges: hence there is no place for complacency either. The clouds lingering on the horizon are far from benign. For example, the factors that have spurred private consumption — GST returns and clipped income taxes — which, in turn, led to a spike in investments, cannot be expected to last in perpetuity. The progress of the monsoon — there are doubts concerning its benevolence — would have an impact on agricultural output and, hence, on prices. Additionally, there is the red eye of Donald Trump’s tariffs — these were imposed in July. And inflation, as always, continues to cast a long shadow. Would the RBI be compelled to tweak rates that have been left unchanged? More importantly, given the prevailing economic uncertainties, would India have the appetite to usher in structural reforms that could ignite the economy further? The answers to these questions could decide how India’s GDP performs in the following quarters. One swallow, as the adage goes, does not quite make a summer.

editorials.title: Where the fiscal squeeze really begins
editorials.passage:
In a diverse federation like India, the state is the primary agent of development. Yet its sub-national governments carry roughly two-thirds of the country’s expenditure responsibilities while commanding only a fraction of its revenue powers. That mismatch is the root of the fiscal squeeze the states repeatedly lament, and it has deepened since 2017, when the GST folded much of their tax autonomy into a shared pool and left them more transfer-dependent than before. Borrowing ceilings cap what they can spend, a transfer mechanism tilting steadily from untied grants towards conditional, tied schemes narrows what they can choose. The states, in short, have far less room to manoeuvre than their budgets suggest.

The usual debate about that room stops too early. It fixates on committed expenditure, and treats whatever is left as freely spendable. The irony is that the real constraint begins precisely where the committed-expenditure discussion ends. India’s fiscal squeeze is structural, not merely a matter of political choice. Incumbents everywhere want to spend to retain power, but the federal system leaves so little headroom that profligacy is more constrained than the rhetoric admits, which is exactly why states reach for increasingly innovative fiscal workarounds.

The deeper story is not about any one government’s politics, it is about how India raises and spends public money. We profess fiscal decentralisation, the structure delivers something closer to its opposite. Most of what the states spend is not freely chosen but imposed, by the constitutional division of subjects, Finance Commission awards, the grants-in-aid framework, and a thicket of statutory and central mandates. The recent white papers released by the incoming Kerala and Tamil Nadu governments make the point in plain numbers.

The standard gauge of a state’s fiscal space is the ratio of committed expenditure, salaries, pensions and interest, to revenue receipts. In Tamil Nadu these three heads now absorb ₹1.89 lakh crore, or 64.4 per cent of revenue receipts, with interest alone at ₹67,050 crore, eating up 22.8 per cent. In Kerala the same trio consumes 77.6 per cent. Read conventionally, the story ends here. a state spending two-thirds to three-quarters of its income on staff, retirees and creditors has little left to deploy.

But the committed-expenditure frame flatters reality. It implies that everything after salaries, pensions and interest is discretionary, money a finance minister can direct at will. That is the illusion the white papers, read carefully, dismantle.

Beneath the headline ratio lies a thick stratum of obligations no government can switch off, yet which appear nowhere in the committed-expenditure number. Grants to local bodies, mandated by State Finance Commission awards and constitutional design, typically claim 4-6 per cent of revenue receipts. The state’s matching share in Centrally Sponsored Schemes is effectively compulsory, since to decline your share is to forfeit the Centre’s, costing another 4-6 per cent. Add the bill for honouring judicial orders, regulatory compliance, the recurring cost of conducting elections and mandated disaster-management spending (together roughly 1-2 per cent), and the government’s own contribution to the National Pension System (1-2 per cent). Individually modest, together these add an estimated 10-15 per cent of revenue receipts on top of committed expenditure for an average state, and considerably more for a stressed one (Chart 1). None of it is committed in the accounting sense; all of it is non-negotiable in practice. Layer on the migration of transfers from untied to tied schemes, and the freedom to allocate shrinks further still.

Whatever sliver survives must still finance the promises that define a government. The strain already shows: developmental expenditure has slipped to 61 per cent of total spending, from 67 per cent before the pandemic (Chart 2). Food and welfare subsidies, pensions for the vulnerable, scheme outlays for education, health and housing, grants for creating capital assets, and the unglamorous but unavoidable cost of maintaining a vast stock of public infrastructure, these are not luxuries but the substance of governance, and the basis on which both governments were elected. Yet they must be funded from a discretionary space squeezed to a fraction of what the headline numbers imply.

Capital formation bears the brunt. When the inflexible layer swallows the revenue account, capital spending becomes the residual, the first thing cut. And as Chart 2 shows, the squeeze is uneven: states carrying larger revenue deficits feel the heat most, their effective fiscal space compressed hardest.

Tamil Nadu and Kerala reach that point by different routes. Tamil Nadu’s debt has nearly doubled, from ₹5.13 lakh crore in 2020-21 to about ₹10 lakh crore in 2025-26, and ₹13.18 lakh crore once public-sector liabilities are counted. Its revenue deficit, at ₹78,324 crore, is the highest in the state’s history. Kerala carries ₹5.07 lakh crore in outstanding liabilities, a heavier 35.5 per cent of GSDP.

In relative terms Kerala’s 77.6 per cent committed ratio is the more alarming, reflecting a large pension and salary bill against a slow-growing revenue base. Tamil Nadu’s bigger economy gives it marginally more headroom on paper (64.4 per cent), but its scale of borrowing and its ₹67,050-crore interest bill expose the weight of its debt. The figure that should anchor the debate, though, is neither committed ratio. It is the share of revenue locked up by the full non-discretionary layer, closer to 87 per cent in Tamil Nadu and an estimated 90 per cent in Kerala.

Three conclusions follow. First, fiscal space is mis-measured: the effective residual, not the committed ratio, is the governance reality. Second, that residual is squeezed from two directions, a uniform, imposed structural layer common to all states, and a variable committed core that drives the differences between them. Structure and discipline are not rivals but entangled: structure sets the pressure, discipline shapes the response. Third, capital formation is the shock absorber that takes the strain, which makes the cost of today’s welfare spending intertemporal, the state keeps paying for welfare while ceasing to build the capacity to deliver it.

The rupee a state government spends, in other words, was rarely free to begin with. Until the debate moves from the committed ratio to the effective residual, we will keep misreading both the squeeze and the states that live inside it.

The writer is Assistant Professor, Gulati Institute of Finance and Taxation. Views are personal

Published on September 2, 2026

editorials.title: Logistics intelligence
editorials.passage:
For much of modern economic history, national competitiveness was shaped by visible infrastructure. The investments in roads, ports, railways and warehouses investments enabled production to scale, markets to integrate and firms to reach customers at lower cost.

The next frontier of logistics competitiveness, however, will not be defined by physical capacity alone, but by the quality of information that allows such capacity to be discovered, compared, trusted and used. Logistics is entering an intelligence-led phase in which data may become as critical to economic performance as concrete, cranes, carriers and containers.

The economic principle is “markets work better when information moves faster than goods”. When logistics assets, routes, capacities, service capabilities, compliance conditions and performance records are visible, firms make better choices. Better logistics intelligence reduces search costs, shortens decision cycles and improves economic outcomes.

Conversely, when information is fragmented, incomplete or inaccessible, the economy pays a hidden tax. Trucks run empty. Warehouses remain underutilised. Firms overstock to protect against uncertainty. Smaller service providers remain invisible to larger customers. Investors misread demand signals. Governments spend on infrastructure without a full picture of utilisation. These are not merely operational inefficiencies. They are economic leakages.

The economics of logistics intelligence therefore rests on five connected principles: reduction of information asymmetry, lower transaction costs, higher asset productivity, better capital allocation and stronger network effects. Together, these principles explain why countries and companies are investing in shared logistics data systems rather than relying only on asset expansion.

Global experience supports this logic. Singapore shows that logistics intelligence can become a source of national competitive advantage. Its PORTNET system links a large community of port and logistics users and enables high-volume digital coordination across shipping, port, freight and trade processes. The economic lesson is that information became a shared infrastructure for users who needed faster, more predictable and more coordinated movement.

The United States adopted a similar principle through Freight Logistics Optimization Works, a public-private partnership in which participants share logistics data and receive aggregated, anonymised visibility into demand, supply and throughput. The user benefit is that companies can look beyond their own operational silos. They cananticipate congestion, align capacity with demand and improve resilience before disruptions become costly.

Japan’s collaborative logistics initiatives point in the same direction. Faced with labour shortages, ageing demographics and rising delivery complexity, Japanese firms are exploring shared standards, common platforms and higher vehicle utilisation. The economic response is not only to add more vehicles or labour, but to make use of existing capacity through better coordination.

The European Union’s electronic Freight Transport Information regulation, or eFTI, shows that governments now view logistics information as economic infrastructure. The eFTI provided a framework for the electronic exchange of freight transport information between businesses and authorities.

Hamburg’s Port Community System demonstrates how shared logistics information can improve coordination and transparency across thousands of participants in the port ecosystem.

For India, this debate is timely. The National Logistics Policy, PM Gati Shakti, Unified Logistics Interface Platform (ULIP) and the Logistics Data Bank have strengthened digital integration and decision support. ULIP has facilitated over 160 crore digital transactions, while the Logistics Data Bank has tracked over 10 crore EXIM containers.

The economic benefits are clearest when viewed from the user’s side of the market.

For manufacturers, logistics intelligence translates into lower delivered cost, better route choices, more reliable partners and improved working-capital efficiency. When transport uncertainty declines, firms can reduce buffer stocks, shorten fulfilment cycles and serve wider markets with greater confidence.

For MSMEs and exporters, the gain is market access. Smaller firms often lose competitiveness because they cannot easily identify dependable warehousing, freight forwarding, cold-chain or multimodal options. A visible logistics ecosystem lowers search and verification costs, allowing smaller enterprises to connect more easily to national and global value chains.

For logistics service providers, the benefit is demand discovery. Regional transporters, warehouse operators, technology firms and specialised service providers can become visible to new customers. This increases utilisation, reduces idle capacity and enables smaller operators to participate in more organised supply chains.

For investors and infrastructure developers, logistics intelligence improves capital allocation. Data on demand clusters, industrial corridors, service gaps and utilisation patterns helps investors place capital where economic need is real. This reduces the risk of stranded assets and accelerates investment into productive logistics capacity.

For governments, it strengthens policy targeting. Better visibility enables public agencies to identify bottlenecks, prioritise infrastructure, monitor corridor performance and design interventions that improve competitiveness rather than merely expand capacity.

For the economy as a whole, these user-level gains compound into larger outcomes: higher asset productivity, lower logistics cost, faster trade movement, stronger manufacturing competitiveness, improved export readiness, better resilience and more inclusive participation by smaller enterprises.

The future of logistics, therefore, is not merely about moving goods more efficiently. It is about enabling economies to use resources more intelligently. That may well become one of the defining drivers of competitiveness in the decades ahead.

The writer is Director General, CII
