There is nothing wrong with any of that. But can we not pause, even for a minute, to speak for a woman who was tied to a tree and set on fire? Can we not say that her life mattered?

Women’s organisations and human-rights activists carry a special responsibility here. Their support cannot depend on whether they approve of a victim’s clothes, language, profession or social-media content. Women’s rights mean little if they are reserved for women who are quiet, “respectable” and easy to defend. The cause must also include women who are loud, unfashionable, controversial or simply unknown. Each is entitled to life, safety and justice. Punjab faced a similar horror in June 2025. Kanchan Kumari, known online as Kamal Kaur Bhabhi, was called to Bathinda for what she was told was a promotional assignment. Police say she was strangled and her body was left in her car. The alleged motive was moral policing: some men decided that her videos were vulgar and that they had the right to punish her. The man named as the alleged mastermind was deported from the UAE, and a Bathinda court has framed murder charges. The case is still before the court. Also Read: Kanchan Kumari was killed for giving men what they want. And that’s the real obscenity When victims are put on trial The two crimes are not known to be connected. The motive in Manjeet’s case is still unclear. Yet the public response to both cases reveals the same discomfort. Instead of beginning with the violence, people begin with the woman. What did she post? How did she speak? What was her reputation? These questions quietly shift attention from the men accused of violence to the conduct of the woman who is dead. After Kanchan’s murder, the Punjab State Commission for Women did condemn the crime, and the police acted against 106 social-media accounts that supported or justified it. Those actions mattered, but they did not produce a broad and lasting campaign across political parties, women’s groups, universities, civil society and the Punjabi entertainment world. The silence became even more disturbing when Giani Malkit Singh, then head granthi of the Akal Takht, reportedly said that “nothing wrong” had happened. Neither Sikhi nor any other religion gives a man the right to pass a death sentence on a woman because he dislikes her videos. Guru Nanak asked, “ So kio manda aakhiye, jit jammeh raajaan ?” — why call her inferior, when kings are born from her? A faith that challenged the low status given to women cannot be used to defend their murder. Sikh institutions should have answered the reported remark immediately and without qualification. These two murders warn us how quickly a woman can be judged, blamed and harmed, and how easily society may put her conduct on trial instead of protecting her. A society cannot call itself progressive merely because it has shiny malls, luxury cars, smartphones and successful women in a few high offices. Its progress is measured by how safe ordinary women feel, how quickly the police act when they are threatened, and whether the public stands with them when they are attacked. A society that does not care for its women has no claim to being progressive. Social-media threats and open praise for murder must be treated as warning signs, not dismissed as online noise. The rest of us also owe something to the seven-year-old boy who has lost his mother in one of the cruellest ways imaginable. He should grow up knowing that she mattered, that women spoke for her, and that society demanded justice instead of placing his mother’s life on trial after her death. Poonam Khaira Sidhu is a former IRS officer, University of Michigan–trained LLM and economist, and published author with articles in international journals and Indian newspapers, specialising in international tax and public policy. Views are personal. (Edited by Asavari Singh)

After Kanchan’s murder, the Punjab State Commission for Women did condemn the crime, and the police acted against 106 social-media accounts that supported or justified it. Those actions mattered, but they did not produce a broad and lasting campaign across political parties, women’s groups, universities, civil society and the Punjabi entertainment world. The silence became even more disturbing when Giani Malkit Singh, then head granthi of the Akal Takht, reportedly said that “nothing wrong” had happened. Neither Sikhi nor any other religion gives a man the right to pass a death sentence on a woman because he dislikes her videos. Guru Nanak asked, “ So kio manda aakhiye, jit jammeh raajaan ?” — why call her inferior, when kings are born from her? A faith that challenged the low status given to women cannot be used to defend their murder. Sikh institutions should have answered the reported remark immediately and without qualification. These two murders warn us how quickly a woman can be judged, blamed and harmed, and how easily society may put her conduct on trial instead of protecting her. A society cannot call itself progressive merely because it has shiny malls, luxury cars, smartphones and successful women in a few high offices. Its progress is measured by how safe ordinary women feel, how quickly the police act when they are threatened, and whether the public stands with them when they are attacked. A society that does not care for its women has no claim to being progressive. Social-media threats and open praise for murder must be treated as warning signs, not dismissed as online noise. The rest of us also owe something to the seven-year-old boy who has lost his mother in one of the cruellest ways imaginable. He should grow up knowing that she mattered, that women spoke for her, and that society demanded justice instead of placing his mother’s life on trial after her death. Poonam Khaira Sidhu is a former IRS officer, University of Michigan–trained LLM and economist, and published author with articles in international journals and Indian newspapers, specialising in international tax and public policy. editorials.title: In a new book, a journalist tries to understand India’s deep suspicion of Hindu-Muslim couples
editorials.passage:
On a hot May evening in 2025, I arrived at the office of the superintendent of police in Uttar Pradesh’s Sambhal district. The journey from Delhi had been long, but the sight of seasonal blooms, a mix of bright red gulmohar and white champa that lined the entrance, instantly re-energised me.

Outside the main building situated in Bahjoi, the administrative headquarters of the district, half a dozen constables were scattered around the gate, twiddling their batons. The gatekeeper pointed towards a parking spot under the shade of an old mango tree. “Desi aam – local variety,” one of the constables sitting in a small room outside the premises told me with pride.

I looked up once again. The mango tree indeed was one of the biggest I had seen. It explained the earlier sweet smell. “Sir [referring to the SP] really likes greenery ,” he added. Then, he pointed towards a nearby jamun tree.

I spent a few minutes familiarising myself, making small talk about crimes in the area with the inspector and support staff I met at the gate. The entrance led through a waiting room with rows of stiff, synthetic chairs designed to look like sofas meant for complainants and visitors.

The room was well-kept, with a high ceiling and a large glass-top desk at the centre. I had walked in expecting a defensive officer in khaki . There was no uniform in sight. Instead, the SP wore a printed T-shirt and trousers, having just returned from outside. I was greeted with warmth and a few pleasantries. He didn’t rush to speak. His soft-spoken composure felt oddly gentle for the authority he represented. Sitting firmly, it seemed as if the SP was already thinking of answers. Clearly, he too had made the time for this conversation.

When I first reached out to him, he was in his native village in Rajasthan, but he promised to meet the following week. True to his word, once he was back in town, we fixed a time. The day we finally met, he looked unmistakably prepared for the subject but began elsewhere. Sighing, he said, almost wistfully, “ I could only visit my hometown for a day.” Clearly, the pressures of the job rarely allowed for more.

At some point, he even asked about my background, perhaps wanting to assess the purpose behind my visit, perhaps also to build some trust. It’s a good sales principle , I remember thinking to myself. Know your consumer before you make the pitch. I had a long list of questions prepared in an attempt to understand the challenges the local police faced while dealing with love jihad cases, especially given the politics around it. But the SP sidestepped most of them during our early conversations. Instead, Bishnoi veered towards what he called disparity. “The Muslims who are rich, they’re very rich. Well off. Very well educated,” he said. “But the rest …” His voice trailed off and his sentence dissolved into silence.

I quickly made peace with his initial reluctance to talk about love jihad. The complexity of his post was not lost on me. For a civil servant, especially one stationed in a communally sensitive district, the stakes are high.

Under the banner of women’s safety, the Yogi Adityanath-led BJP government in UP has rolled out both token and structural measures, ranging from anti-Romeo squads to dedicated women’s helplines and functional mahila thanas in every district. At a 2021 rally in Prayagraj, Prime Minister Narendra Modi claimed that under BJP rule, women in UP now had both “security and rights”, praising Yogi’s tough stance on crimes against the state’s “sisters and daughters”.

Given the volatility of the subject, and the tightrope SP Bishnoi and others like him walked between following the law and being answerable to men in high political chairs, sometimes against their own instincts, speaking too honestly could cost him. I have seen the weight of these pressures up close.

The same officer, talking about the challenges on the ground, spoke of a local case where the girl had moved to a nearby city from her home in the village and started living more freely – “open-minded”, as he put it. When she met a Muslim boy in the city, she fell for him. The boy allegedly didn’t disclose his religion until much later.

“The girl was from a financially weak family and emotionally caught up. He invited her to stay with him, supported her with money. She was lured. When the family found out, they came running to the thana. Then the pressure began. Politicians, activists, media. And let me tell you, ladkiyan bhi kam nahin hoti hain [even girls are no less now]. In the name of freedom …” While concluding, he said, “In today’s age, many girls also know their rights and they push back. It becomes a full-blown ‘mahila apradh’ matter [women-related crime]. We have to act on high priority.” He rattled off sections of the IPC as if flipping through a dossier.

Every love story turned into a case file. Every complaint is a ticking clock under political scrutiny. Law and order and women’s rights are two of the main poll planks used by the BJP in Uttar Pradesh and so there is an image to be maintained.

Back in Bishnoi’s office, he was careful, cautious not to say anything that could sound too controversial. After all, just a few hundred metres from his office stood the Shahi Jama Masjid, one of the oldest surviving Mughal-era mosques in Uttar Pradesh, built in the early sixteenth century during the reign of the empire’s first emperor, Babur.

In late 2024, a local court ordered an archaeological survey of the premises after claims were made about the mosque having been constructed over a temple’s ruins. The survey order alone was enough to stoke fear and anxiety in the area. The feelings were rooted in precedent.

Since the Ram Janmabhoomi movement and the demolition of the Babri Masjid in Ayodhya in 1992, any suggestion that a mosque might be sitting atop an older temple structure has been politically volatile. Although the Supreme Court’s 2019 Ayodhya verdict awarded the disputed site to Hindu claimants, it had also reiterated the sanctity of the Places of Worship Act, 1991, which bars the conversion of religious places and freezes their religious character as it stood on the eve of the country’s Independence on August 15, 1947.

The court had called the act a vital safeguard of secularism in India and declared that it “imposes a non-derogable obligation towards enforcing our commitment to secularism under the Constitution.” Yet in the years that followed, several high-profile cases, whether in Varanasi’s Gyanvapi, Mathura or now Sambhal, have been testing that boundary.

People remembered what had happened in Ayodhya and how it had begun: first with claims of buried temples, then court-monitored surveys, and eventually, large-scale demolition followed by communal violence. The survey order at Shahi Masjid was enough to stir that memory, inflame old tensions and raise the chilling possibility of another rupture.

After the court ordered this survey, protests broke out almost immediately in Sambhal and things quickly took a violent turn. The reaction by the protesters was passionate and the police responded. Some people died. Dozens were injured. Internet services were cut overnight. Tear gas filled the cold November air and all this had taken place just about six months before my visit.

When I sat down to interview the SP, I had imagined a dramatic story, one day in the life of a cop tasked with chasing love jihad suspects. I thought of dossiers, nighttime raids, court files stacked on desks, suspicious couples picked up late at night and brought to the thana, and intense interrogations of Muslim boys accused under the love jihad law. But the reality was far less cinematic. In fact, there were barely any cases.

I was here because I wanted to expose this reality. So I asked him directly, “I mentioned this the other day as well [over the phone] about forced conversions. Since the ordinance came into effect in early 2021, I’m trying to map what’s changed. How has the law actually played out on the ground? What’s the situation with acquittals, convictions, active cases?” He told me, “There have been no convictions yet. But we are expecting convictions of a few criminals in one or two very strong cases. They are ongoing in court …” He gave a half-shrug and started explaining himself. “See, it’s a small town,” he began. “There’s a lot of migration, boys going out for work, families shifting. And then, sometimes, girls are, well, whatever way they are taken. Some fall in love, some just … leave. But in a town like this, where there’s so much animosity between two communities, even one such case becomes volatile. It can be coloured as communal. It becomes challenging.”

I asked him, “When a case comes to you, say, for kidnapping as I’ve often heard, is sometimes elopement labelled kidnapping?” He perked up, suddenly animated, eager to confirm what I’d said.

“Yes, yes! Exactly! That’s how most of these begin. Kidnapping is the first word. Even when the girl is above 18, even if she has run away by choice, if the family disagrees, it’s kidnapping.” He repeated this several times, as if to reinforce that I had hit upon something “accurate”.

I pressed on. “But there are also cases where the girl hasn’t left by choice, right? Where consent is disputed. How do you judge that? How do you find merit in a case?” He leaned forward slightly, his voice growing more conspiratorial. “There are cases,” he said, “where a boy will say his name is Raju. But later, we find out his name is Riyazuddin. Could be anyone. Raju is a very neutral, very safe name . ” I didn’t interrupt. “They use that name. They talk, they befriend the girl. They say they’re in love. And then later, once the attachment has built, they say, ‘Actually, my real name is something else.’”

Excerpted with permission from Under A Saffron Sky: Inside India’s Crackdown On Love, Ismat Ara, Penguin India.

editorials.title: Will Rahul Gandhi’s ‘smash the patriarchy’ call attract young, urban women to Congress?
editorials.passage:
Vaishnavi Patil, 26, was supposed to share the stage with Rahul Gandhi at a Congress party event for women in Pune last month. She could not address the crowd because of time constraints but was far from disappointed.

“This was the first event where a political party head was talking about women-centric issues,” the researcher told Scroll after the event.

More than a thousand kilometres away in Delhi, the significance of what happened in Pune was not lost on Kritika Jain either. The 22-year-old psychology graduate said that she was “shocked” to see a male politician talk about the patriarchal nature of Indian society.

“Oh my god! Wow! Is this for real?” she remembered thinking when she came across snippets from Gandhi’s speech on Instagram. “When I thought about it more, I was actually impressed.”

Scroll spoke to young women from several Indian cities and found much the same sentiment. Clearly, Gandhi had struck a chord with a constituency that is otherwise neglected in Indian politics: young, urban women.

However, most interviewees were quick to add that statements alone would not make them vote for the Congress party in future elections. They wanted to see Gandhi and his party do more for women before they decided to get behind him.

In Pune, Gandhi took a stridently feminist tone in his hour-long address to the crowd of mostly young women. Some attendees also joined him on stage and voiced their concerns.

“You do not belong to anybody except yourself,” he declared, drawing loud cheers. “You have a relationship with your father, husband, brother, son. But you do not belong to them.”

The public meeting in Pune was the fourth in a series of concert-style rallies through which Gandhi has been trying to appeal to young Indians. His party is calling the campaign Chhatron Ki Goonj, or echoing students’ voices. This was the first time that his presentation focused on women and the pitch was largely successful: his message resonated with many of the women at the venue.

Diya, an 18-year-old law student at Pune’s Bharati Vidyapeeth College, was convinced that the leader of opposition in the Lok Sabha knew what women wanted. “If he comes to power, we are going to get more solutions for our problems instead of them being dismissed,” she said.

The Congress already fares better among urban women as compared to rural women, according to data put out by Lokniti, an election studies programme of the Delhi-based Centre for the Study of Developing Societies. In the 2024 Lok Sabha elections, for example, 21% rural women voted for the party, while 35% of them preferred the Bharatiya Janata Party. But the gap between the two parties narrowed for urban women, 25% of whom voted for the Congress, whereas 36% went with the BJP.

It is no surprise then that the grand old party is trying to close this gap further.

Journalist Ruhi Tewari, author of a book titled What Women Want: Understanding the Female Voter in Modern India , calls Gandhi’s outreach a new sort of politics that tries to move beyond welfare.

Till now, Indian politicians have pursued women-oriented schemes such as incentives for girls’ education, free cooking gas connections and cash transfers. But Tewari suggested that those benefits had now become the baseline for many young women who were looking for more. Gandhi’s call to “smash the patriarchy” was meant to appeal to them.

“This younger woman is looking for not just welfare delivery,” Tewari said. “She is more interested in looking at questions of representation, questions of equality.”

This was evident at the event in Pune, where some of the middle-class women in attendance expressed dissatisfaction with the Maharashtra government’s Ladki Bahin Yojana. The scheme provides Rs 1,500 every month for women between the ages of 21 and 65, if their families make less than Rs 2.5 lakh a year.

“How is Rs 1,500 going to help when I earn Rs 25,000?” asked Patil, the researcher quoted earlier in this piece. “What are you doing for me – for working women?”

The BJP has largely avoided responding to Gandhi’s main point and has so far focused on the references he made to the Manusmriti , an ancient Hindu legal text, during his address in Pune. The chief ministers of Assam and Uttar Pradesh have criticised the Congress leader for singling out Hinduism while talking about patriarchy.

Political scientist Suhas Palshikar was not surprised by this, considering the importance that “cultural pride” holds in the Hindutva imagination.

“This attack on Manusmriti or any attack on any part of our present existence, which requires an introspection into the past, is unacceptable to them [the BJP],” he explained.

However, the young women from different Indian cities, whom Scroll spoke to, did not seem to buy the BJP’s argument.

Aishwarya Dwivedi, 30, agreed with Gandhi that gender discrimination might be enshrined in some Hindu scriptures. She had herself experienced how Hindu families expect women to perform religious rituals, but their husbands are often exempt.

“He [Gandhi] is hitting the right notes,” said the software consultant who lives in Bhopal. “All the women around me know that they are victims of patriarchy. So, what he has brought up is very close to a lot of women’s hearts because they see it on a daily basis.”

Gandhi’s popularity among younger women may also be driven, in part, by the way he carries himself. Jain, the 22-year-old psychology graduate from Delhi, admitted to finding him “hot and sexy”.

“I get a few reels of his thirst traps on my Instagram and I don’t mind that,” she added laughingly. “There is a sense of personality and charisma. You can make edits on him using catchy songs. It is kind of difficult to do that with Modi.”

The Congress leader, too, appears to be playing to this gallery of late. On Instagram, he recently opened up about his fitness routine , for example. Since June, when the Chhatron Ki Goonj campaign began, he has ditched his usual white shirt on several occasions and opted for colourful ones instead.

While all of this may be getting Gandhi more attention from young women, it alone will not win him their votes. Jain, the woman from Delhi who called him “sexy”, said that she wanted to see him do more to empower women before voting for him.

Dwivedi, the software consultant from Bhopal, was more direct. “I don’t care about his pookieness,” she stated, referring to the internet slang of endearment that some use for Gandhi online.

She had also come across his Pune speech on Instagram. She then went looking for his full presentation and was disappointed to find no “actionable items” in it. The Congress could work on including gender sensitisation in school curriculum, she suggested, giving the party a year’s time to convince her to vote for it.

Srinidhi Vardhan, a 21-year-old marketing professional from Chennai, was just as unconvinced about voting for the party even though she admitted that the event in Pune had roused her curiosity.

“This will not be the turning point after which I will want him [Gandhi] to win,” she said. “But it will make me look more into what he is doing and follow what he will be up to in the coming days.”

Tewari, the journalist, was of the view that Gandhi should increase women’s representation in the Congress party if he wanted to earn credibility among women. She reasoned that it was not enough for the grand old party to blame the Modi government for intertwining the law mandating 33% reservation for women in legislatures with the controversial delimitation process.

“The act should be implemented, but why must any political party, including the BJP, wait for it?” Tewari asked. “What is stopping him [Gandhi] from saying that the next election onwards, he will ensure that women get as many tickets as men do, or at least 33% tickets? It would help his cause greatly.”

Political analysts contend that the Congress leader will likely struggle to rally support from his party when it comes to taking any concrete steps towards gender equality.

Veteran journalist Neerja Chowdhury, who has covered Gandhi’s political career as well as that of his mother, father and grandmother, appreciated him for delivering a “strong message” in Pune, but then also pointed to the ramshackle state of the Congress party.

“I have always felt that Rahul Gandhi is enamoured of social change,” Chowdhury noted. “He has got that NGO element in him. The problem is that while he is creating a buzz, the Congress’ organisation is virtually non-existent in many states. Winning elections is not only about creating a narrative.”

Palshikar, the political scientist, agreed. The Congress, he said, comes up with ideas that attract media attention and get intellectuals and activists “keyed up”, but does not have the machinery to sustain the momentum on the ground.

According to him, even in states where the Congress does have its organisational structure in place, Gandhi confronts a recurring problem: his party does not share its leader’s enthusiasm for progressive ideas such as gender equality.

“The real hurdle is the mindset of the so-called party stalwarts,” Palshikar argued. “Everywhere, the Congress is controlled by them rather than Rahul Gandhi. If you look at the BJP, once they get the cue from the top, everyone starts believing the same thing right down to the bottom.”

With inputs from Tanya Shrivastava and Johanna Deeksha.

editorials.title: Mankind destroyed whatever was gifted as life: Tagore’s lament for the environment 87 years ago
editorials.passage:
About a century ago, long before environmental degradation became the crisis of our times, Nobel Laureate Rabindranath Tagore had sounded early warning bells about the destruction of forests.

Though Tagore was born in the city of Kolkata, he had a deep and abiding contact with nature from childhood, and it shaped his many-sided genius in diverse ways. As an adolescent, he accompanied his father Debendranath to the foothills of the Himalayas, an experience he wrote about in his autobiographical notes.

Later, he was a frequent visitor to a zamindari estate in Shilaidaha, now in Bangladesh, where many of his short stories and songs were written while on a boat on the mighty river Padma. He had experienced the vast expanse of nature – in the sky, in the mountains, in the rivers and the flat, verdant lands of the Bengal delta.

Simultaneously he witnessed the urbanisation of the sleepy villages around Kolkata and Kolkata itself, and lamented the oppressive bounds of concrete and the lessening of contact between human beings and nature. When he founded his school, now a part of the Central University, Visva-Bharati, Santiniketan, a Unesco World Heritage Site – he ensured that classes took place under canopies of trees rather than within the confines of four walls.

Tagore is widely known as a romantic poet but he was also a social thinker, deeply interested in advances in science and their application for the betterment of human societies. He formed village cooperatives, sent his son Rathindranath to study science-based agricultural studies in the United States, and began to explore modern methods and their viability in local conditions at Sriniketan, a few kilometres from Santiniketan.

His concern for the environment blended with an awareness of the needs of an urbanising population. This conflict between the demands of an urbanising, industrialising world and the imperative to preserve our bond with nature is a recurrent theme in his work – most powerfully, perhaps, in the play Raktakarabi (Red Oleanders), where the life-force of nature, embodied in the character of Nandini, confronts the dehumanising machinery of an underground mining kingdom.

With these concerns in mind, Tagore had initiated the Vriksharopana Utsav – the annual festival of tree planting – at Sriniketan, alongside the Halakarshana, the ceremonial ploughing of the fields. On September 2, 1938, he gave a lecture at the annual celebration of this tree planting festival. That lecture, translated here for the first time into English, is strikingly relevant – the prescience of a sensitive and great mind.

In the first phase of creation, the earth was rocky and barren. There was no hint of her compassion to any form of life around her. In all directions the volcanoes were erupting; the frequent earthquakes made the ground unquiet. While this was going on, in an unforeseen, auspicious moment, the goddess of the forest sent her messengers to this theatre of the earth. The green grass began to cover what was naked; slowly, shrubs and trees appeared as harbingers of life. Animals were still not upon the scene. In order to welcome and nurture the incipient and precious life, the trees made their own food and provided shade upon the ground. Their greatest gift was to harness the fiery rays of the sun and to store them for future consumption by mankind when, much later, human beings would make their appearance. Even now our civilisation continues to advance drawing from the same source of life and energy.

Human beings are prone to being wasteful. As long as they roamed in the forests, they maintained a rich, meaningful, balanced interaction with nature. As they began to form settlements, they started to lose their sense of belonging with the forests. The human beings forgot their very first set of friends who brought to the earth the original and the divine gift of life; instead, they began to attack the forests in the most cruel and thoughtless manner so that they could make their own homes built with wood, bricks and mortar. By ignoring the blessing brought by the primordial green trees, human beings invited upon themselves a curse to spread.

Today, parts of northern India are becoming arid and suffering from extreme heat during the summer months. But anyone familiar with the old texts would know that these areas were once covered with forests where the hermits would stay in their simple but beautiful dwellings in the cool shade of tall trees. Human beings dealt with the gift of nature like a vulture; unhappy with the bounty offered to them, they destroyed the forests without any care in the world. Deforestation is leading to gradual desertification. If we are to avoid a calamitous end for ourselves, we have to recall the divine spirit which gave us the boon of the forests and pray that the life force that once sustained us, may the same life force protect our land; may it give us shade for comfort and fruits for sustenance.

The problem has not cropped up specifically for us or just today. Everywhere it is a great challenge to save the treasures of forests from the devouring greed of mankind. In the United States too, the timber industry has destroyed forests resulting in sand blown storms destroying fertile fields. The creator of the universe had sent the messenger of life and made arrangement for its nourishment, to which the human beings added the ingredient of death borne out of greed.

Human society has been subjected to so much curse because of its superseding the divine intention to nurture life. Wanton self-indulgence and consequent loss of forests have brought about gaping, self-inflicted wounds. Those trees which provided the canopy of leaves that would purify the air, the great mass of fallen leaves which would make the ground fecund, they have been uprooted. Whatever was gifted as life to the good earth, mankind oblivious to its own good has destroyed these very things.

It is now time to repent. Though our resources are limited, we will employ them to build an altar to welcome back in our midst the divine forest spirit of life. Our meagre beginning today has two parts. First is tilling the fields; tilling the fields to meet our needs; our needs for food grains. Tilling the land is our unavoidable duty to ourselves. But we must give something back in return so that we lessen the damage caused to the earth. To redress her wounds, to replenish what we take, we have organised the festival of planting trees. It is our earnest hope that the seeds we sow today, the saplings that we plant today will grow into green fields and beautiful shady trees which will make this little corner of our world with fruit laden forests and verdant fields serene and beautiful.

Utpal Chattopadhyay, a mathematician and teacher from Kolkata, translates and writes essays illuminating different precious stones strewn around in Bengali literature. He can be reached via email at utpal.ch@gmail.com .

September 2 is the 87th anniversary of Tagore’s ‘Lord of the Forest’ address.

editorials.title: More Indian students are abandoning higher education as degrees no longer seem worth the cost
editorials.passage:
While the youth protests were underway at the Jantar Mantar in the first week of July, the Central government published two crucial reports on higher education enrollment: the All India Survey on Higher Education for 2022-’23 and 2023-’24.

The findings were alarming. For the first time since 2011, there has been a decline in the number of Indian students pursuing undergraduate degrees. In 2023-’24, undergraduate enrolment decreased by 93,321 students compared with the previous academic year, representing a decline of 0.29%. This decline at national level might look small. But for a developing country like India enrollments for higher education are supposed to grow fast.

Maharashtra was among the states with the sharpest declines: 5% of Class 12 students here did not enroll in the undergraduate enrollment. This means that nearly 200,000 fewer young people in the state opted for degree programmes compared to the previous year. The number dropped from 35,04,046 in 2023-’24 from 36,88,956 in 2022-’23.

The case of Maharashtra is striking, as it is one of the most industrially advanced states in the country. It is home to cities such as Mumbai, Pune, Nashik and Aurangabad which provide jobs in the manufacturing and service sectors. The declining importance of degrees among young people in such a state is telling because a graduate degree is a prerequisite for good jobs in the organised sector.

Is it possible that these youth simply pivoted to short-term, skill-based certificate or diploma courses? Unfortunately, this is not the case. The same government report shows only an insignificant increase in enrollment in diploma and certificate courses.

Why would the vast majority of Maharashtra’s youths turn their backs on higher education and why has this number suddenly swelled?

The answer lies either in a waning enthusiasm for education or a decline in the financial capacity of their parents – two factors that are inextricably linked.

Most parents evaluate further education as an investment of time and money. If this investment does not yield better employment opportunities and stable jobs, they inevitably question its necessity. When household incomes stagnate or fall, the probability of abandoning higher education rises sharply.

In the United States, for instance, approximately 64% of high school graduates enroll in degree-granting institutions (which formally encompass both two-year associate degrees and four-year bachelor’s programmes). This is nearly double India’s rate of gross enrollment ratio for higher education. Across most developed nations, participation in formal post-secondary education is more than twice that of India – and the quality of education delivered is significantly superior.

Ironically, the AISHE data was released against the backdrop of reports about the Central government reducing education expenditure as a percentage of the gross domestic product.

The decline also makes it clear that graduate degrees have lost their “signaling value”. Theoretically, a degree serves as a signal to the job market, guaranteeing that the holder possesses the knowledge and skills necessary for employment. However, due to the plummeting standards of Indian colleges, degrees have been reduced to a mere minimum formal requirement rather than vouching for a student’s actual competence.

Under the present regulatory system, establishing innovative educational institutions that impart the modern skills and knowledge demanded by the market is nearly impossible. Established institutions are shielded from genuine competition. They face no pressure to raise their teaching standards, to update their curricula or to offer innovative teaching methods. As a consequence, passionate educational entrepreneurs are systematically demoralised.

Instead, this regulatory framework has been exploited by politicians, who have emerged as the largest suppliers of new educational institutes in the country. This is a dominant cause of the collapsing quality of higher education.

Indians often complain about the “commercialisation of education” but this is true only in a limited sense. In a truly free market, poor quality is punished. But in India’s distorted system, institutions can easily survive – and even receive encouragement to expand – without ever providing high-quality education.

When the signaling value of a degree diminishes relative to the money and time invested, turning away from higher education becomes a highly rational economic decision for parents and students. They simply choose to exit a broken system. Against this incredibly bleak backdrop, the Cockroach Janata Party effectively placed the quality of education on the political agenda. It is imperative that it stays there for the long haul.

Milind Murugkar writes on economic and social issues.

editorials.title: Delhi Brics summit: Can the elephant and the dragon dance together?
editorials.passage:
Just think about it. The sequencing of the handing over of personal invites from Prime Minister Narendra Modi to both his Russian and Chinese counterparts to attend the Brics summit in New Delhi is a bit unusual and perhaps of some significance. Why was NSA Ajit Doval sent to Beijing to give the personal invite and interact with Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi? Why could External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar not have been told to do the job? Jaishankar was, as a matter of fact, in Moscow around that time presenting the invite to the Brics summit to President Vladimir Putin. Jaishankar could have quite easily gone over to Beijing after his visit to Moscow and given the invite. What was the need to send Doval?

Next question. A few weeks back, we were told that Chinese President Xi Jinping would in all probability not be able to come to India for the Brics summit. And then suddenly, after the Doval-Wang meeting, we get news that Xi may be coming to India, and that too with a massive 400-member business delegation in tow. What then changed on the ground? Is some breakthrough of significance in Indo-Chinese ties, be it business or military, on the anvil?

Is this flurry of unusual diplomatese somehow connected to American interactions with both Beijing and New Delhi? Before we deep-dive into this possibility, let us understand the compulsions and priorities of both China and India, especially in their individual, different and difficult relationships with America.

The Indian dilemma in its relationship with America is this. We just cannot figure out the US of today under the leadership of President Donald Trump. We are not clear what America really wants from us and where this ‘defining partnership of the 21st century’ is headed. The relationship is like a Richter scale, never at rest. Peaks and troughs, peaks and troughs. Let’s take the positives for starters. President Trump has, on not one but many occasions, called Prime Minister Modi a ‘dear friend’. President Trump’s man in New Delhi — Ambassador Sergio Gor — is perpetually on ‘Bharat darshan’. He has visited important defence, civilian and even space infrastructure; met Indian political personalities and chief ministers of states on both sides of the aisle. And after every meeting, he has expressed optimism about the future course of India-US ties. The trade deal, he keeps repeating, is ‘nearly finalised’.

Now, if one were to shut out the white noise of actual geopolitics on ground zero and only listen to Ambassador Gor’s utterances on India-US relations, then we are in a rose-tinted, milk-and-honey phase between both countries. The truth, however, is a little more unpalatable and stark.

India has had the dubious distinction of being practically the first-ever country to come under the hammer of overbearing American presidential tariffs — the toughest ever in recent mercantile history. India’s arch-enemy, Pakistani Field Marshal Asim Munir, has been serenaded by President Trump countless times on the world stage. The US is sparing no effort to choke cheap and plentiful Russian oil supplies to India. The H-1B visa programme, enabling and benefiting technologically skilled Indians seeking work in the United States, has all but been killed by the new administration. The list of aggressive American actions impacting India in so many ways, often adversely, is never-ending.

At the other end of the spectrum, China has fared no better. President Trump has often waxed eloquent about President Xi Jinping, but no one has any illusions that President Trump wants to put China in its place, disrupt its oil supply from Iran, and overcome American dependency on Chinese supply chains and imports of critical minerals. To say the Chinese are feeling the pain of a changed world order would be understating it. In short, President Trump, unlike any other American President before him, has shaken and rattled the world order beyond recognition.

The Doval visit to Beijing, then, might have been a first step to identify, discuss and agree upon some very limited areas of commonality between India and China to face up to a rampaging America. Call it a hedging of bets for both countries to face up to an America unrecognisable in its present avatar compared with the past. And no better place to firm up these understandings than the Brics summit, representing 45 per cent of the world’s population and 35 per cent of global GDP. And perhaps take the first, tentative baby steps towards a life beyond the US dollar.

We are, of course, in the realm of speculation and joining the dots out here. There is no official version of what could have transpired in the Doval-Wang dialogue. The cue that talks of some significance were held with a degree of success in Beijing is that the Chinese President may now attend the Brics summit in Delhi and Doval, an expert in security architecture, was picked over Jaishankar to initiate those talks.

So, then, the million-dollar question: an agreement on what exactly? Perhaps this question is best answered by what will never be agreed upon in the short run. There might not be a big-bang border breakthrough announcement during the Brics summit. The likely convergence could be no more salami-slicing of border territories initiated from the Chinese side, unfettered patrolling rights for Indian soldiers at agreed points, expedited and frequent border resolution talks at senior army levels and, above all, abundant caution for China not to repeat a Galwan to advance Chinese-style military morality.

India has publicly stated that the relationship, including the commercial side, would only normalise once the vexed border issue is resolved. But the above-mentioned agreement points could be a starting point for India. The fact of the matter is both countries can hedge their bets against America, perhaps even stand up to it, once the Americans discover that both China and India are not warring militarily and their trade and commerce have gone up exponentially. If that happens, there could be a softening on the American side towards both countries.

This, of course, does not mean India and China would stop shadow-boxing against each other. India will aggressively build maritime defence ties with Japan and other powers in the Indo-Pacific. It will pitch more deadly variants of the feared BrahMos missile to the Philippines, Indonesia and Vietnam and play its own game of encircling China in the South China Sea. China will, of course, go all out to arm Pakistan and Bangladesh against India.

And yet all this could change in the future if this tepid agreement between China and India at next month’s Brics summit survives and sustains the passage of time. India-China trade now is valued at $155 billion. The day and time this trade doubles and quadruples, China will have no choice but to let go of Pakistan and take India very, very seriously. That is the key to this imbroglio.

Till then, there will be no waltz. The two countries, in the meantime, have of course entered the dance floor and both sides are measuring each other up. The waltz is still some distance away.

(Juggi Bhasin is a veteran TV journalist, author and geopolitical commentator, with his commentary featuring in The CAA Show on YouTube. Views presented are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect Firstpost’s views.)

editorials.title: China’s Tibet mega dam: India’s concerns should go beyond a ‘water weapon’
editorials.passage:
On August 26, a glacial collapse above the Lhende Khola in Nepal’s Rasuwa district sent a surge down the Trishuli, tragically killing over a thousand people across Nepal and Tibet, sweeping away 32 bridges, and damaging fourteen hydropower and solar projects. The notice period was scant because any upstream sensors were rapidly destroyed. Further, the flash-flood early warning system, jointly maintained by Chinese and Nepali scientists for years, performed poorly because its water-level monitors had been calibrated for monsoon and perennial flooding rather than for a sudden ice-and-rock avalanche. Chinese dam activity in Tibet seems to be off the hook — for now.

In January 2025, I argued that the 60 GW project approved by Beijing at the Great Bend of the Yarlung Tsangpo — the Medog Hydropower Station — did not warrant the securitised reaction it received in India. That case rested on three propositions. First, China’s contribution to the Brahmaputra’s volume, once rainfall in Assam and Arunachal is accounted for, lies somewhere between 7 and 30 per cent. Second, using a dam of that scale as a so-called tap would degrade Tibet’s own ecology and displace Tibetans before it impacted anyone downstream. Third, the announcement could be considered an investment play in the final budgetary year of the 14th Five-Year Plan — with PowerChina, the lead SOE behind the construction of the dam, as the primary beneficiary. Nothing since then has been falsified, except that the project has moved well beyond being just a proposal.

Since Chinese Premier Li Qiang’s visit to Nyingchi for a sort of first-brick-laying ceremony in July 2025, the project has announced five cascade stations across roughly 250 kilometres and an investment figure of about 1.2 trillion yuan ($170 billion). The project’s target is about 300 billion kilowatt-hours annually, and it is expected to be fully commercially functional by the early 2030s. The operations of the project have been handed over to the China Yajiang Group, which comes under the auspices of State Council-supervised central enterprises.

There are three concerns that such a dam project generates, the worst consequences of which are a widespread disaster and many casualties. First is the issue raised by the construction area being one of the most seismically active zones on Earth. The engineering of the dam is such that it requires a drop of nearly 2,000 metres over 50 kilometres, achieved by tunnelling through the Namcha Barwa massif. It lies roughly 50 kilometres from the McMahon Line, and India has seen the downstream consequences of the Yigong landslide dam of April 2000, which sent a flood into Arunachal Pradesh that killed around 30 people and left over 100 missing. That was an unengineered blockage that took two months to give way. A cascade of five stations failing in sequence would release far more water on far less notice, and the first Indian authorities would know of it would be when the Siang began rising at Pasighat.

Second, there is again an issue similar to that observed in the case of the Nepal floods — information and notification flow is meagre. Since it expired in 2023, the India-China Brahmaputra data-sharing MoU has not been renewed. Beijing has previously demonstrated a willingness to suspend such sharing for reasons unrelated to hydrology. During the 2017 Doklam standoff, data was sent to Bangladesh, but not to India. On the Yarlung Tsangpo, too, if there is no standing channel of communication, India has almost no time to prepare or respond because heavy waters would already have reached Pasighat.

At this point, spending diplomatic capital on reviving the MoU is only meaningful if it can extract from China its seasonal and annual plans for the run-of-the-river dam. The dams planned for the lower Yarlung Tsangpo are run-of-the-river structures rather than storage models akin to the Three Gorges Dam, meaning they generate power from the river’s fall rather than from water held behind a wall. Thinking of the Medog project’s weaponisation potential as a tap, hence, helps less. The important information on which any meaningful counteraction rests is knowing the amount of water China plans to take upstream to push through the turbines, because that is what will determine how much water is subsequently released downstream.

Third, there is the question of India’s level of preparation itself. It has proposed the Siang Upper Multipurpose Project explicitly to counter Chinese construction upstream. But that would place a large storage structure in the same seismic belt, notwithstanding the fact that it has been stalled because of sustained local opposition in the Siang valley. Downstream readiness does not need one vulnerability to counter another and can rely on embankments, gauging stations on the Siang and Lohit rivers, and, of course, modelling for worst-case scenario events.

(Anushka Saxena is Associate Fellow, Geostrategy Programme, the Takshashila Institution. Views presented are the author’s and do not represent those of the Institution. They do not necessarily reflect Firstpost’s views.)

editorials.title: India’s 7.8% GDP Growth: Is the Government’s Data Really What it Seems?
editorials.passage: The Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI), the Government of India’s statistical agency, released the first-quarter 2026-27 (Q1-2027) gross value added (GVA) and gross domestic product (GDP) estimates on 31 August.The press release issued by MoSPI claimed that India’s real GDP recorded growth of 7.8 percent in Q1-2027, compared with growth of 6.9 percent in Q1-2026. In nominal terms (at current prices), the GDP recorded growth of 10.3 percent in Q1-2027 against growth of 8.1 percent in Q1-2026, the press release further said.Everyone seems to be overjoyed as the growth numbers beat everyone’s estimates, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) included. Prime Minister Modi called this “exemplary growth” and a “herculean feat.” Finance Minister Sitharaman saw this as proof of continuous government reforms and agile economic management. The Chief Economic Advisor (CEA) found India’s strong first-quarter GDP growth a demonstration of the economy’s continued resilience against global headwinds.The growth of 7.8 percent in Q1-2027, in the face of turmoil in the oil and gas market thanks to the completely unjustified US-Iran war, does look great optically. But is it real?Last year, in the press release on 29 August 2025, MoSPI/GoI had estimated Q1-2026 growth at an identical 7.8 percent, which has now been revised down to 6.9 percent. Is the downward revision in last year’s growth primarily responsible for the higher growth? Or are there deeper mechanics at work, including the retrofitting of last year’s first-quarter numbers to boost the growth rate to a seemingly respectable 7.8 percent?New Robes for India’s GDP: The Reality of Modi Govt's Growth StoryThe press release issued on 31 August 2026 places India’s first quarter 2026-27 GDP in current prices at Rs 88.27 trillion. The same press release estimates India’s first quarter 2025-26 GDP in current prices at Rs 80.00 trillion. This yields growth of 10.3 percent. The first quarter GDP for 2024-25 has been estimated at Rs 74.03 trillion, making the Q1-2026 growth of GDP in current prices 8.1 percent. The Q1-2027 GDP growth at 10.3 percent is certainly higher than growth of 8.1 percent in Q1-2026, given higher inflation in the current year.The nominal GDP for Q1-2026, however, was not Rs 80.00 trillion with a growth rate 6.9 percent when the GDP press release was issued last year in August 2025. The Government had claimed that India had achieved a higher real GDP growth rate of 7.8 percent. The GDP at current prices in Q1-2026 was estimated at Rs 86.05 trillion in the August 2025 press release. Yes, Rs 86.05 trillion and not Rs 80.00 trillion, to which it has now been revised.Government growth estimates/claims go for a toss drastically the moment you compare this year’s GDP (in current prices) with that of GDP (in current prices) for the same quarter announced last year. The GDP of Rs 88.27 trillion in Q1-2027 is only 2.6 percent higher than the GDP of Rs 86.05 trillion in Q1-2026. Yes, only 2.6 percent.That lowly growth shows an awfully poor GDP performance in the Q1-2027 in current prices. If you take even a 2 to 2.5 percent inflation/deflator factor in the 2026-27 first quarter over the same quarter last year, the real GDP growth completely disappears, reducing it to zero (not 7.8 percent as claimed).The government has been using this toolkit for the last few years, of over-projecting GDP in the concerned current year by showing high GDP growth in current prices and low or no inflation. In 2024-25 also, the Q1 GDP in current prices, which was announced at Rs 70.25 trillion in the press release of August 2024, has been reduced to Rs 66.81 trillion. It may be recalled that the government had revised down the 2023-24 GDP (current prices) by as much as Rs 11.4 trillion (from Rs 301.23 trillion to Rs 289.73 trillion) when the new series of GDP was issued earlier this year. The method is simple. Revise down the GDP of the year gone by to show the present year’s performance in much better colours. No one cares to see this revision of last year’s numbers, is the time tested belief. Don’t be surprised if the 2026-27 first quarter GDP is revised down next year (in August 2027) to show the 2027-28 Q1 performance better. If one were to compare the Q1-2027 performance for the eight GVA sectors against their claimed GVAs last year, a messy and horrifying picture emerges. Agriculture, mining, and electricity sector GVA growth shoots up sharply (much higher than what the MoSPI press release says). Agriculture had GVA of Rs 12.00 trillion in Q1-2026. It has grown to Rs 14.00 trillion in Q1-2027, giving a year-on-year (YoY) growth of 16.7 percent. Mining GVA grew from Rs 1.36 trillion to Rs 1.78 trillion, generating growth of 31 percent. Electricity GVA went up from Rs 2.04 trillion to Rs 2.29 trillion, yielding a growth of 12.2 percent.Construction and financial services, taking Q1-2026 GVA, as per the August 2025 press release, show much smaller growth in Q1-2027. Construction (Rs 6.77 trillion if not revised to Rs 6.24 trillion now) would have given a growth of 7.27 percent (instead of 16.5 percent as per the 31 August press release) and financial services (Rs 20.71 trillion if not revised to Rs 19.34 trillion) would be only 5.3 percent higher (in place of 12.7 percent).The worst performance is in:ManufacturingTrade, hotels, transport, communications, services groupsPublic administration sectorsThe downward revision of their GVA in Q1-2026 from Rs 10.92 trillion to Rs 9.61 trillion, from Rs 12.28 trillion to Rs 10.53 trillion and from Rs 12.17 trillion to Rs 9.96 trillion respectively has led to improvement in their GVA growth from -5.2, -2.2 percent and -9.2 percent (actual) respectively to a high of 7.7 percent, 14.0 percent and 11 percent (as claimed in the 31 August press release) respectively.On the expenditure side, the major downward adjustment has been made to private consumption (PFCE). It has been revised for Q1-2026 from Rs 51.87 trillion to Rs 44.66 trillion, resulting in a negative consumption growth of as much as -5.4 percent in relation to the PFCE of Rs 49.08 trillion. That perhaps explains why the pain of weak consumption felt in real life has got hidden in these restated numbers. The gross capital formation expenditure (GFCE), having been revised down marginally, would have still yielded impressive growth of 15.5 percent as against 20.4 percent claimed by MoSPI.Why did MoSPI decide to revise down the sectoral GVA for Q1-2026 so sharply and violently? The current GDP/GVA numbers are not supposed to vary so widely as these are sourced from the actual corporate and other government data. Did the selective application of double digit deflator do the trick or there were some other motivations at work? GDP Growth Without Tax Boom: The Real State of Revenues, Expenditures & DeficitsThe stock market sold off today. The RBI, after enabling considerable foreign exchange inflows through quite costly mechanisms, did heavy lifting to see that the rupee appreciate somewhat. Foreign investors keep selling.The government did everything it could do to ensure that capital expenditure was kept up for GFCF to report better (there is no real momentum on the private capex side, though).It does not really do the Indian economy any good if these designer numbers are served to impress the people. The economy is in a difficult spot. It is better to recognise it and set about taking all necessary corrective and reform steps instead of pulling the wool over everyone’s eyes.(Subhash Chandra Garg is the Chief Policy Advisor, SUBHANJALI, and Former Finance and Economic Affairs Secretary, Government of India. He's the author of many books, including 'The $10 Trillion Dream Dented, 'We Also Make Policy', and 'Explanation and Commentary on Budget 2025-26'. This is an opinion piece, and the views expressed above are the author’s own. The Quint neither endorses nor is responsible for the same.)
